vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti groups 'klāsa' within the knāsādi quadruplet (knāsa, jñāsa, krāsa, klāsa) with the meanings of motion ('gati') and propitiation or accomplishment ('rādhanam'). It follows standard Bhvādi formation with Guṇa and Seṭ augment, yielding forms such as klāsati, caklāsa, and klāsitā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'klāsa' conveys either 'gati' (movement) or 'rādhanam' (to gratify, appease, or achieve). It is an unaccented vowel root taking the Seṭ iṭ-augment across non-sarvadhatuka affixes.

meanings.English: to move, go, please, propitiate, or accomplish

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root svad primarily means to taste, relish, or to be pleasant and delicious to the palate. It operates in the Atmanepada in its primary active conjugation, forming 'svadate'. When used in causative (Nic), it conveys making something flavorful or causing someone to taste.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy relishes the sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother sweetens the medicine with honey.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti records 'svada asvadane' under the Bhvadi-gana. Being anudattenta, it takes Atmanepada affixes. It denotes the act of tasting, experiencing flavor, or being pleasingly palatable. The forms like svadate, sasvade, and svadita are derived regularly with the intermediate augment 'it'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'svada asvadane' as relishing or appreciating taste (rasanubhava). It is noted as anudattet and set, yielding standard Atmanepada forms in the sarvadhatuka tenses without irregular stem modifications.

meanings.English: to taste, relish, or be pleasing to the palate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tvac' means to cover, wrap, or conceal something. In simple present active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent directly covering or clothing an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The tree covers itself with bark.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the child to be covered with a cloth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses 'tvaca saṃvaraṇe' as an action of encompassing, covering, or shielding. It is classified under the Bhvadi class, taking regular Parasmaipada terminations with intermediate 'i' (set) in non-sarvadhatuka forms.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'tvaca saṃvaraṇe' as 'ācchādana' (clothing, covering, enveloping), noting its nominal kinship to 'tvac' (skin, bark, outer protective layer).

meanings.English: to cover, to wrap, to shield, to enclose

canonical_dhatvartha: sthirībhāve pratiṣṭhāyāṃ ca (to be firm, to stand on firm ground)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sthal' belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvadi-gana) and takes Parasmaipada endings. It signifies coming to a halt, establishing oneself on dry or firm ground, or being steady. When used in the simple present tense (Kartari Prayoga), it describes the subject becoming firm or resting in a stable position. In the causative (Nic), it shifts to 'sthālayati', meaning to establish or make someone/something stay firmly on a place.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense / Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: stands firmly / settles on firm ground
scenarios.example_english: The traveler stands firmly on the ground for rest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The sailor docks and secures the boat firmly onto the shore.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses 'sthala' in the sense of 'sthirībhāve' (achieving stability, firmness) and 'pratiṣṭhāyām' (firm establishment). As an akarmaka (intransitive) root of the Bhvadi class, it takes the Shap vikarana yielding the present base 'sthala-' with Parasmaipada terminations (sthalati, sthalataḥ, sthalanti).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini records 'sthala sthirībhāve pratiṣṭhāyāṃ ca', emphasizing the attainment of a solid base or state of rest on dry or immovable ground. It forms the past participle 'sthalita' and periphrastic forms following the standard set conjugation rules.

meanings.English: to stand firmly, to be established, to settle on firm ground
meanings.Hindi: sthir hona, jamna, sthan grahan karna
meanings.Bengali: sthir haoya, sthan labh kara, sthapita haoya
meanings.German: feststehen, sich festsetzen, festen Boden fassen
meanings.French: se fixer, se poser fermement, s'etablir

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mrad' belongs to the Bhvadi gana and takes Atmanepada terminations in its non-causative state to describe the action of crushing, rubbing, grinding, or pulverizing an object. When transformed into the causative (Nich) form, it describes causing another person or instrument to pound or crush something into powder or pulp.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana, kartari prayoga (Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer crushes the herb on the stone slab.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nich pratyaya, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (Causative Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The physician makes the pupil grind the medicinal ingredients.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mrada mardane. mardanam curnikaranam vinasho va. anudattetvabhavad api anudattannitastang iti siddhe atmanepadi. set. mradate, mamrade, mradita, mradishyate, amradishta. nyante tu jnajanijanashanjashranjnamiti mit-samjnavikalpat hrasva-dhirghayor vikalpah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mrada mardane. mardanam vishleshanam pechanam ca. mradate, mamrade. set. atmanepadam. nich-sannantatveshu rupa-visheshah pradarshitah.

meanings.English: to crush, grind, pulverize, rub, trample, soften
meanings.Kannada: hudi madu, mardisu, churna madu, tudidu
meanings.Telugu: naluputa, churna cheyuta, mardinchuta, podi cheyuta
meanings.Hindi: masalna, peesna, choor karna, mardan karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sphur' means to throb, quiver, twitch, or suddenly flash/glitter. In the basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an automatic or natural twitching, pulsing, or shining. In the causative form, it means to make something throb, burst forth, or distinctly reveal/manifest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Simple Present Active)
scenarios.example_english: The eye twitches.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The lightning flashes light in the darkness.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'sphura' is read in the sense of 'sphurana' (quivering, flashing, throbbing). In sarvadhatuka affixes, the vowel undergoes guna or remains based on operational sutras, producing forms like sphurati. In ardhadhatuka contexts, optional it-agama applies in specific non-lit formations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'sphura sphurane' denotes quick intermittent motion, vibration, or sudden visual flashing like sparks or lightning. The primary parasmaipada form is established as sphurati.

meanings.English: to throb, quiver, twitch, flash, glitter

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ghrā' means 'to smell' or 'to perceive scent'. In regular non-causative present tense (Sarvadhatuka), the root ghrā undergoes a special substitution to become 'jighra-', taking standard Parasmaipada endings. When someone causes another to smell, or when causative 'ṇic' is added, it becomes 'ghrāpayati' or 'jighrapayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person single)
scenarios.example_english: The boy smells the flower.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the baby smell the fragrant fruit.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes 'ghrā gandhopādāne' belonging to the Bhvadi class. In Sarvadhatuka environments like Lat, Lot, Lan, and Vidhilin, rule 'ghrā-dhmā-sthā-mnā...' (7.3.78) applies, substituting the stem with 'jighra-'. In perfect tense (Lit), it forms 'jaghrau'. Being anit, it does not take i-agama in Ardhadhatuka forms.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains that 'gandhopādānam' signifies smelling through the olfactory sense (nāsikayā gandhagrahana). It is anit, parasmaipadi, and exhibits stem replacement as jighrati, jighratah, jighranti.

meanings.English: to smell, perceive fragrance, sniff

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛt' primarily denotes the action of wrapping, winding, encircling, or weaving around an object. In its simple present active form (kartati), it describes a subject enveloping or binding something. When used in the causative form (kartayati), it signifies causing someone else to wrap, bind, or intertwine a material.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Lat Lakara (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd wraps the staff with a string.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to wrap, spin, or wind
scenarios.example_english: The master makes the servant wind the cloth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṛtī' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with an indicatory long 'ī' denoting anit properties in certain contexts and saṃveṣṭana (surrounding, entwining, wrapping). In the general active present tense (Lat), the guṇa vowel replacement yields the base form 'karta-', leading to the third-person singular realization 'kartati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'kṛtī saṃveṣṭane' that the primary semantic import is vestanam or bandhanam (covering, surrounding, or binding around). It follows regular Bhvadi paratva with the suffix Shap, forming 'kartati' through standard medial ar-guna.

meanings.English: To wrap, to entwine, to envelop, to wind around

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mluc' primarily denotes motion (going, moving, or slipping away). When used with specific prefixes such as 'ni-', it commonly conveys the specialized meaning of setting or sinking below the horizon (as of the sun).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Active Voice), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer slips away towards the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga with the upasarga 'ni' (downward motion/setting)
scenarios.example_english: The sun sets behind the mountain.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'mlucu gatau' under the Bhvadi-gana. It details the gunated present form 'mlocati' with the vikarna 'sap', notes alternative grammatical traditions allowing nasalization ('mlancati'), and documents the lit form 'mamloca'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini glosses 'mlucu gatau' alongside 'mruc', emphasizing movement, evasive motion, or gradual disappearance/setting as seen in celestial and natural contexts.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to slip away, to set (like the sun)
meanings.Bengali: jaoa, chola, adrishya haoya, osto jaoya
meanings.French: aller, se deplacer, se coucher, disparaitre

canonical_dhatvartha: bandhane sparshane ca (in the sense of binding, obstructing, or touching)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pas' belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvadi) and uses Parasmaipada endings. Its base action means to bind, fasten, or touch closely. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it shifts from merely binding or touching to causing someone or something to be bound or tethered.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Lat Lakara (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd binds the cow with a rope.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to bind or secures firmly through someone
scenarios.example_english: The master makes the servant tie the animal.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'pasa' is categorized in Bhvadigana with the semantic marker 'bandhane sparshane ca'. As an adanta-stem forming a basic thematic anga with shap, it takes the standard guna-free form 'pasati'. It is inherently transitive and inflects in the active voice.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'pasa bandhane', pointing out that the verbal action denotes fastening, embracing, or obstructing, sharing semantic roots with the nominal derivation 'pasha' (a snare or bond).

meanings.English: To bind, tie, fasten, or touch
meanings.Bengali: Badha, bandhana kora ba sparsha kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root dr̥bh means to string together, arrange, compose, or weave into a coherent structure. In the present tense, it forms 'darbhati' (or 'dr̥mbhati' when taking idit-like nasalization in specific recensions), showing an active agent composing or stringing items together. Adding the causative prefix/suffix (niċ) creates 'darbhayati', meaning causing someone to arrange or string words/flowers together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Laṭ lakara, Prathama-puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The poet composes/strings together a verse.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Niċ), Kartari prayoga, Laṭ lakara, Prathama-puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/She causes (someone) to string together or compose.
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the disciple to compose a treatise.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'dr̥bha sandarbhe' denotes the act of methodical composition, stringing together, or tying into order (sandarbha / granthana). Being aniṭ in standard Bhvadi enumeration, it takes guna in sarvadhatuka contexts yielding 'darbhati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin classifies the root under the sense of sandarbha (composition/arrangement). He elaborates that forms like 'sandarbha' (textual context, connected discourse) are nominal derivatives conveying cohesive structuring of words or objects.

meanings.English: to string together, weave, arrange, compose

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dam' primarily means to be quiet, tame, calm, or restrained. In standard active usage (Kartari Prayoga), it describes a person or animal becoming pacified or subdued. When combined with the causative suffix (Nic), it becomes transitive ('damayati'), meaning 'to tame, control, or subjugate someone else'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara (Present Indicative), Active Voice
scenarios.example_english: The sage becomes calm and free from anger.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Prena (Causative - Nic Pratyaya), Lat Lakara
scenarios.example_english: The king subdues the enemies.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'damu upaśame' belongs to the Bhvadi class. By the rule 'śamām aṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani', lengthening of the penultimate vowel occurs when followed by the affix 'śyan', yielding forms like 'dāmyati'. In the primary sense of upashama (cessation, calmness, self-restraint), it functions as an intransitive root.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'damu' under the group of calming/restraining roots (upaśamārtha). It notes that in the simple present it exhibits the characteristic lengthening of the 'a' vowel in specific conjugational patterns and signifies inward tranquility, self-control, and the cessation of agitation.

meanings.English: to be calm, to be tamed, to practice self-restraint
meanings.Telugu: shantinchuta, indriya nigrahamu kaligi unduta, damanamagu
meanings.Hindi: shant hona, indriyo ko vash me karna, daman hona
meanings.Bengali: shanto howa, indriya songjom kora, domito howa
meanings.German: sich beruhigen, sich bezahmen, beherrscht sein
meanings.French: se calmer, s'apaiser, etre dompte ou maitrise

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dāś' primarily means 'to give', 'to grant', or 'to offer an oblation/gift'. In active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject performs the act of offering or giving. When used with the causative suffix (ṇic), it conveys causing someone else to offer or distribute a gift.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana)
scenarios.example_english: The devotee offers sacred oblation to the deities.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana)
scenarios.meaning: causes to give / makes someone offer
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the student to give charity.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dāśṛ dāne. dāśati, dadāśa. dānārthe vartamānaḥ sakarmakaḥ aniṭ parasmaipadī.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dāśṛ dāne. dāśati haviḥ. dāśanaṃ dānamityarthaḥ.

meanings.English: to give, to grant, to offer, to bestow

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'de' carries an anubandha 'ṅ' (deṅ), which makes it take Atmanepada verb endings. In the present tense, the vowel 'e' changes to 'ay' before the conjugation suffix 'a', forming 'dayate'. It primarily conveys the sense of protecting, guarding, or having mercy/compassion upon someone. When made causative with the suffix 'ṇic', it forms 'dāyayati' meaning 'causes to protect'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The king protects the citizens.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, parasmaipada, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to protect / makes someone guard
scenarios.example_english: The master causes the servant to guard the house.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'deṅ rakṣaṇe' is anudātta-et and ṅit, hence strictly Ātmanepada. By the application of the rule 'adeṅ guṇaḥ' and standard sandhi rules with the vikaraṇa śap, the root becomes 'dayate' in the present tense. It is seṭ in the ardhadhatuka categories, taking 'iṭ' agama.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'deṅ rakṣaṇe' under the Bhvadi-gana. The root means preservation, protection, and extending compassion. Forms such as dayate, dayāñcakre, and dayitā are derived accordingly.

meanings.English: to protect, guard, defend, cherish

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khell' belongs to the Bhvadi class and means 'to move' or 'to waver/shake'. It takes standard Parasmaipada endings with the thematic affix 'shap' (a), forming 'khellati' in the present tense. In the causative (nic), it takes the meaning of 'making something move' or 'shaking something'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Simple present active)
scenarios.example_english: The leaf sways due to the force of the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The breeze causes the branch of the tree to shake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: khellr calane - idam acalane 'pi kvacit dhrshyatiprayoge bhavishyati. idit-karanam prayojanavirahat. khellati, cikhella, khellita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: khellr calane. calanam gatih kampanam va. khellati, cikhella. seyam calanartha-santatih.

meanings.English: to move, to sway, to shake

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vañc' originally means to move slowly, make small movements, or dodge. In everyday usage and causative forms, this idea of crooked or evasive movement evolves to mean dodging someone or deceiving/cheating them.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer dodges from the hunter.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative/extended form), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The rogue cheats the innocent person.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'vañcu' is listed with the meaning 'gatyalpatve' (diminished, slight, or crooked motion). Madhava notes the application of specific nasal-elision and optional it-agama rules across various kridanta formations such as vañcitva and vakva.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'gatyalpatve' as moving in a subtle, meandering, or slow manner, which classically serves as the semantic base for avoidance, evasive maneuvers, and figurative deceit.

meanings.English: to move slowly, to go crookedly, to dodge, to deceive
meanings.Hindi: dheere chalna, bach nikalna, thagna ya dhokha dena
meanings.Bengali: dhire chola, phanki deoya, bonchona kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'math' primarily means to churn, agitate, or shake vigorously. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), the agent performs the action of stirring or destroying. When the causative suffix nic is added, it means to cause someone to churn or distress deeply.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd girl churns the curd.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to churn or severely torments
scenarios.example_english: Grief torments his mind.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'matha vilodane' as an action of vigorous movement and stirring (alodana), yielding the present base form 'mathati'. Being anit in classical derivation without idagama in standard non-sarvadhatuka environments, it forms 'mamatha' in lit-lakara and 'mathisyati' or 'manthisyati' depending on id-agama options in particular contexts.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'matha' denotes physical agitation, churning liquids like milk or curds, and metaphorically crushing or tormenting adversaries. It belongs to the non-id (anit) consonant-ending group in the core Bhvadi paradigm.

meanings.English: to churn, agitate, stir, crush, harass

canonical_dhatvartha: sancalane (in the sense of moving, shaking, or playing)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khel' means to move, swing, or play. In its simple form, it expresses normal moving or sporting by a person or object. When made causative (khelayati), it means to cause someone else to play, or to toss/shake something around playfully.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Parasmaipada, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The boy plays in the garden with a ball.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Parasmaipada, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The mother amuses the child (causes the child to play).

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'khelr' belongs to the Bhvadi class and takes the canonical meaning of 'sancalane' (shaking or moving about). Being an anudattopadesha root with an indicatory 'ri' (ir-it/r-it), it forms its present base with the affix Shap, yielding 'khelati' in the active voice.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'khelr' as 'khelr calane'—signifying bodily motion, sport, or wavering movement. It is set (takes intermediate i in certain non-conjugational tenses) and inflects in the Parasmaipada.

meanings.English: to play, to sport, to move, to shake

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dīṅ' belongs to the First Gana (Bhvadi) and means to waste away, diminish, or decay. Because of the marker letter 'ṅ' (Nit), it takes Atmanepada endings in basic conjugations. When used in the simple present tense, it describes an entity undergoing natural decline or diminishing. When combined with the causative suffix (Nic), it changes meaning to causing something to diminish or wearing something out.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi Lat lakara (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular), Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The physical body diminishes due to the effect of time.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: causes to waste away / reduces / diminishes
scenarios.example_english: The disease reduces his physical strength.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'dīṅ kṣaye' as an anit, anudatta-it, ṅit verbal root in the Bhvadi gana. The marker letter 'ṅ' mandates Atmanepada affixes by the rule 'Anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam'. It explains the morphophonemic alterations in Sarvadhatuka forms yielding 'dayate' and periphrastic/causative variations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshiratarangini defines 'dīṅ' strictly in the meaning of loss, exhaustion, or gradual deterioration ('kṣayo hrāsaḥ'). It highlights the distinction between this root and homophonic roots in other classes, noting its anit characteristic in non-periphrastic Ardhadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to decay, to waste away, to diminish, to perish
meanings.Bengali: kshoy howa, rhas pawa, khin howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root bhran means to give or distribute. In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent directly giving or bestowing an object to someone. When converted to the causative form (Nic), it signifies causing someone else to give or distribute gifts/charity.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (Kartari Prayoga), Lat lakara (Present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The wealthy person gives wealth to the poor person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Kartari Prayoga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: He causes someone to give / makes someone distribute
scenarios.example_english: The king has the minister distribute food.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root bhraṇa belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read in the sense of dane (giving). It is Parasmaipadi, udattopadesha, and takes the intermediate augment it (set) in non-sarvadhatuka forms. The present tense base forms bhranati with sap.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin classifies bhran under dane alongside sran. It is parasmaibhashi and forms bhranati, babhrana, and bhranita, showing standard Guna and augment it where applicable.

meanings.English: to give, bestow, donate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'cel' describes the act of moving, stirring, or quivering. In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it shows a subject moving on its own. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), the meaning shifts from 'to move' to 'to cause to move' or 'to shake something'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice, simple present tense, lat)
scenarios.example_english: The leaf of the tree stirs due to the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative present tense)
scenarios.meaning: causes to move or shakes something
scenarios.example_english: The monkey shakes the branch of the tree.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'celṛ sañcalane' belongs to the Bhvadi class. Being an ṛdit root (having ṛ as an it-marker), it takes the aṅ affix in the aorist tense (luṅ), resulting in forms like acelat instead of sica-based forms. Perfect tense yields cicela, celatuḥ, celuḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines celṛ in the sense of motion and quivering (calane). Due to its ṛdit status, the aorist exhibits the aṅ substitute without vriddhi of the root vowel (acelat). Regular Parasmaipada conjugational endings apply across standard lakaras.

meanings.English: to move, to shake, to stir, to tremble
meanings.Russian: dvigat sya, shevelit sya, kolebat sya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pā' means 'to drink'. In the simple active present tense (Kartari Prayoga), it replaces its stem with 'piba-' before Sarvadhatuka endings, yielding 'pibati' (he/she drinks). In causative voice (ṇijanta), the stem becomes 'pāyayati' meaning 'causes to drink' or 'gives to drink'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (stem substituted with piba-)
scenarios.example_english: The boy drinks milk.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to drink / feeds liquid to
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the child drink water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: pā pāne. Bhvādi Parasmaipadi anudāttaḥ aniṭ. 'pāghrādhmāsthāmnādāṇdṛśya...' sūtreṇa pibādeśaḥ. pibati, papau, pātā, pāsyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: pā pāne. anudāttetaḥ pibādeśaḥ śiti. pibati, papau, pātā. pānaṃ, pātavyam.

meanings.English: to drink, consume liquids, imbibe

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛt' belongs to the First Gana (Bhvādi) and means 'to wrap, wind, encircle, or spin'. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), the vowel 'ṛ' undergoes Guṇa strengthening to become 'ar', producing forms like 'kartati' (he/she wraps or spins). In causative constructions, the affix 'ṇic' is added to yield 'kartayati', shifting the meaning to 'causes to wrap or spin'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present tense (Laṭ), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The weaver spins the thread.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative active voice (Ṇic + Kartari Prayoga), Present tense (Laṭ), 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to wrap or spin
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the child wrap the cloth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṛtī~' is listed in the Bhvādi-gaṇa with the canonical meaning 'veṣṭane' (wrapping, winding, spinning). The long 'ī' marker denotes specific morpho-phonological properties in kṛt derivations. In Sarvadhatuka environments like Laṭ, Guna applies to the radical vowel ('ṛ' becomes 'ar'), producing the standard base 'karta-' before the affix 'śap', generating 'kartati', 'cakarta', 'kartitā', and 'kartiṣyati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'kṛtī veṣṭane' as kartati, meaning surrounding or enveloping ('pariveṣṭana') as well as spinning threads. He distinguishes this first-class root 'kṛt' (which takes Guna and Parasmaipada) from the sixth-class (Tudādi) homophone 'kṛtī chedane' (kṛntati), which means 'to cut'.

meanings.English: To wrap, to encircle, to spin thread, to surround

transitivity: Intransitive (Akarmaka) / Transitive (Sakarmaka in context of sporting/leaping)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ksvel' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana and means to move about, shake, or playfully leap/sport. In active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes standard Parasmaipada endings with the 'sap' affix, conjugating as 'ksvelati' (he/she moves or sports). When causative 'nic' is added, it forms 'ksvelayati' (causes to move, shakes something).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer leaps playfully in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The wind shakes the branch.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'ksvelr sancalane' as a Parasmaipadi root in Bhvadi-gana. The anubandha 'r' indicates optional forms in specific ardhadhatuka suffixes, conjugated regularly in sarvadhatuka tenses as ksvelati, cikvela, ksvelita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'ksvelr' in the sense of motion, playful movement, and oscillation ('sancalana'). It is grouped alongside related motion and agitation roots like kela, khela, and cela, taking set inflection in classical forms.

meanings.English: to move, shake, tremble, or play/sport

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mlecch' means to speak indistinctly, incoherently, or in an unintelligible/foreign language. In the basic active voice (Kartari Parasmaipada), it simply describes someone babbling or speaking in a manner that is not clearly understood. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it means to cause someone to speak indistinctly or to distort speech.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Kartari)
scenarios.example_english: The child speaks indistinctly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Makes someone speak indistinctly or garbles speech
scenarios.example_english: Intoxication makes the person speak indistinctly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti treats 'mleccha avyaktayam vaci' as an udattopadesha, Parasmaipada, and set root belonging to the Bhvadi class. It notes that the operation denotes speech lacking clarity in phonetics or syntax (aspashta-varnoccarana), deriving the standard primary present form as mlecchati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini clarifies 'mleccha avyaktayam vaci' as the articulation of obscure, corrupted, or non-classical speech (apasabda-prayoga). It derives forms like mimleccha in Lita, mlecchita in Nishtha, noting its regular set conjugation.

meanings.English: to speak indistinctly, to utter unintelligibly, to babble
meanings.Telugu: aspatamuga matladu, ardam kani vidhamuga matladu
meanings.Hindi: aspat bolna, avyakt vani bolna, totlana
meanings.Bengali: asposhto kotha bola, obekto bhabe bola
meanings.Chinese: shuohua bu qingchu, nan yi ting dong de fayin

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'mṛṣ' means to endure, tolerate, or bear patiently. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent enduring pain, harsh words, or difficulties. When converted to the causative form (marṣayati), it means to cause someone to tolerate or to make someone put up with a situation.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple present tense (Laṭ, Kartari Prayoga, Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The wise person endures hardship.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative present tense (Ṇijanta Laṭ, Kartari Prayoga, Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The mother helps the child endure the cold.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mṛṣā' is read with the semantic marker 'titakṣāyām' indicating forbearance or endurance (sahanātmake arthe). Being of the Bhvādi class with Parasmaipada endings, it undergoes guṇa in the present system yielding 'marṣati'. It takes the augment iṭ in standard non-sarvadhātuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mṛṣā titakṣāyām' in the context of patience and suffering without anger (kṣamāyām). The standard derivation gives 'marṣati', 'mamarṣa', and 'marṣitā'.

meanings.English: To endure, bear, tolerate, forgive

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhṛṣ' means to be bold, daring, or courageous. In simple present tense (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent showing confidence or daring to act. When used in causative (dhīrṣayati/dharṣayati), it shifts to 'causing to dare' or 'assaulting/challenging someone'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The brave warrior acts boldly in battle.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The hero overpowers the enemy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhṛṣi~ prāgalbhye - prāgalbhyaṃ dhārṣṭyam uttsāho vā. dharṣati. seṭatvāt dharṣiṣyati idit-lakṣaṇam anumateḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhṛṣi~ prāgalbhye - dhṛṣṇotīti dhārṣṭyavān bhavati. dharṣati, dadharṣa, dharṣitā.

meanings.English: to be bold, to dare, to be courageous, to venture
meanings.Tamil: tuṇivu koḷ, eccarikkaiyōṭu tuṇi, etirkka tuṇivu koḷ
meanings.Hindi: dhīṭha honā, sāhasa karnā, himmata dikhānā
meanings.Bengali: sāhasa karā, dhṛṣṭatā dekhāno, sparddhā karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mṛd' means to experience happiness, delight, or comfort. Because it is Ātmanepadī in the primary sense, the action and its emotional benefit reflect within the subject ('mardate' = he/she delights or feels happy). When converted into the causative form ('mardayati'), it changes to mean making someone else happy or gladdening another person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice, singular, present tense laṭ)
scenarios.example_english: The boy feels happy with his friends.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇijanta (causative present tense)
scenarios.example_english: A noble deed delights the minds of all.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mṛdaँ sukhe' belongs to the Bhvādi class with anudātta marker, making it Ātmanepadī. In the presence of the sārvadhātuka affix 'śap', the vowel 'ṛ' undergoes guṇa to become 'ar', producing the present stem 'marda-' and yielding the form 'mardate'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin glosses 'mṛda sukhe' as being contented, joyful, or in a state of comfort, noting its structural parallel with roots like 'muda harṣaṇe'.

meanings.English: to be happy, to delight, to rejoice
meanings.Hindi: sukhī honā, prasanna honā, ānandita honā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'shuc' means to grieve, mourn, or feel sorrow. In the basic active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an individual experiencing grief or sorrow. In the causative form, it means to cause someone to grieve or to distress someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Kartari Prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The son grieves during misfortune.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic (Causative), Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sad news distresses everyone.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes 'shuca shoke' under Bhvadi-gana. Gunation of the root vowel 'u' to 'o' occurs before Sarvadhatuka affixes yielding 'shocati'. It is fundamentally associated with internal emotional affliction and bereavement.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini explains 'shuca shoke' as signifying torment, heat of grief, or mental sorrow ('shoko manastapah'). It emphasizes its standard Parasmaipada inflection.

meanings.English: to grieve, to mourn, to sorrow, to lament

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vrīḍ' expresses the natural human emotion of feeling shy, embarrassed, or modest. In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a person experiencing shame or shyness. When converted into the causative form (nic), it changes meaning from 'feeling shy' to 'making someone feel shy or ashamed'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: feels shy or blushes with modesty
scenarios.example_sanskrit: bālakaḥ gurūṇāṁ samakṣaṁ praśasitaḥ san vrīḍati.
scenarios.example_english: The boy feels shy when praised in front of his teachers.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to feel ashamed or embarrassed
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person's conduct brings shame upon the family.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'vrīḍṛ lajjāyām' belongs to the Bhvadi class. The final letter 'ṛ' is an it-marker indicating that the root retains its structural properties without specific vocalic changes typical of anudatta roots. As an akarmaka root signifying internal shame and bashfulness, it takes standard Parasmaipada terminations yielding 'vrīḍati' in the present tense and 'vivrīḍa' in the perfect tense.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'vrīḍṛ' under the meaning of 'lajjā' (bashfulness, modest reservation). It is classified as anit/set variations per contextual ardhadhatuka rules where standard seṭ behavior applies in non-exceptional forms (vrīḍitvā), expressing modesty, moral hesitation, or embarrassment.

meanings.English: to feel shy, to be bashful, to be ashamed, to blush

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root tuj means to hurt or strike, to be strong or strengthen, and to dwell or reside. Because the root has an inherent 'i' marker (idit), a nasal 'n' is inserted before the final consonant in general conjugations, producing the base form tuñj-. When converted into the causative form (nic), it changes vowel quality to produce tonjayate or tonjayati, meaning to cause someone to strike or to invigorate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Kartari Prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The warrior strikes the enemy in battle.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Indicative), Causative (Nic), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Kartari Prayoga
scenarios.meaning: causes to hurt, energizes, or strengthens
scenarios.example_english: The commander energizes and empowers the soldiers.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root tuji is listed with the canonical senses of himsa (violence/hurting), bala (strength/energizing), and niketana (dwelling/habitation). Being an idit root, the augment num (nasal) is regularly applied in Sarvadhatuka forms yielding tunjati, tutonja, tonjita, and tonjisyati. In causative contexts, guna applies to yield tonjayati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes tuji as an idit root denoting three specific actions: injury (himsana), strength (samarthya), and living in a place (vasa). The nasal infix is constant due to the anubandha 'i', resulting in the standard verbal form tunjati.

meanings.English: to injure, to strike, to strengthen, to dwell
meanings.Hindi: himsa karna, balvan karna, nivas karna
meanings.Bengali: himsa kara, balaban kara, bas kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mañc' means to hold, sustain, or raise something high (which is also where the word 'mañca' or platform/dais comes from). In normal active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings to express holding or lifting aloft. When using the causative suffix (Nic), it signifies making someone raise or set up a raised structure.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The man raises the flag high.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to elevate or erects a platform
scenarios.example_english: The artisan causes a raised platform to be erected.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'maci' or 'mañci' is listed in the sense of 'dharana' (bearing/sustaining) and 'ucchraya' (raising/elevating). Due to the inherent idit marker, the root takes the num-agama (nasalization) across sarvadhatuka and ardhadhatuka forms, yielding mañcati, mamañca, and mañcita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains that this root expresses the act of lifting up or holding aloft firmly. The derivative noun 'mañca' (a raised couch, platform, or scaffold) is directly formed from this root through the ghan affix, reflecting the core sense of ucchraya (elevation).

meanings.English: To hold, to support, to elevate, to raise high
meanings.Hindi: Dharana karana, uncha uthana, uchha karana
meanings.Bengali: Dharana kara, upare tola, uccha kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dāś' means to give, offer, or make an oblation. In the basic active voice (Parasmaipada), the agent performs the act of offering or donating something to someone. When converted to the causative form (nic), it conveys causing someone to offer or give.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The devotee offers an oblation to the deity.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to give / makes someone offer
scenarios.example_english: The teacher inspires the student to make an offering.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root dāśṛ is anudāttet, carrying the anubandha 'ṛ' to prevent vṛddhi in certain aorist forms or govern specific aṅa-pratyaya rules. It primarily signifies the act of giving (dāna) or making sacrificial offerings (havis-pradāna).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes dāśṛ dāne as an active Bhvadi root signifying giving and worshipping through oblation. The forms conjugate systematically in Parasmaipada like dāśati, dadāśa, dāśiṣyati.

meanings.English: to give, to offer, to grant, to bestow

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhukṣ' means to kindle, stimulate, or endure difficulty. It is an Atmanepadi root, so in standard present tense it takes endings like '-te' (dhukṣate). It is frequently used with the prefix 'sam' (sandhukṣate) to convey rekindling enthusiasm, hope, or fire.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Present tense (Lat lakara), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: He endures hardship during his penance.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'sam' + Kartari prayoga, Present tense (Lat lakara), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The fire blazes up when fanned by the wind.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhukṣa' is read in the sense of sandīpana (kindling, inflaming) and kleśasahana (enduring affliction or suffering). Being anudāttet, it takes Atmanepada affixes and is seṭ (takes the augment iṭ in non-sarvadhatuka environments). Forms include dhukṣate, dudhukṣe, and adhukṣiṣṭa.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'dhukṣa sandīpane', highlighting the meaning of making something blaze or arousing enthusiasm/courage in the mind (utsāhavṛddhiḥ). Typical present indicative form is dhukṣate.

meanings.English: to kindle, to inflame, to endure

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svad' means to taste, relish, or to be pleasing and savory to the palate. In standard present tense (kartari prayoga), it takes Atmanepada endings ('svadate') to show that something tastes good or a person relishes a taste. When combined with the causative suffix nic, it shifts to Ubhayapada ('svadayati' / 'svadayate') meaning to make something tasty, sweeten, or cause someone to taste food.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The sweet fruit tastes pleasing in the mouth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the food tasty with salt.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The dhatu 'svada' is categorized under the Bhvadi-gana with the meaning 'asvadane' (relishing or tasting). It is anudattet and therefore takes Atmanepada affixes. Forms like svadate, sasvade, svadita develop regularly with the augment it (set).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'svada asvadane', highlighting its semantic sphere in experiencing taste or bestowing deliciousness, forming 'svadate' and in causative 'svadayati' (to make savory).

meanings.English: to taste, to relish, to be savory or pleasant to taste
meanings.Russian: probovat na vkus, naslazhdatsya vkusom, byt vkusnym

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hṛ' means to take away, steal, or carry. Because it has an 'ñ' marker (ñit), it is Ubhayapada: use Parasmaipada (harati) when the result of taking benefits someone else, and Atmanepada (harate) when the action directly benefits the subject or is done for oneself. When prefixes (upasargas) are added, its meaning transforms widely (e.g., pra-hṛ = to strike, sam-hṛ = to destroy, vi-hṛ = to stroll).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Parasmaipada (kartari prayoga, general action)
scenarios.meaning: carries away or takes away for others
scenarios.example_english: The servant carries away the load.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Atmanepada (kartrabhiprāya kriyāphala)
scenarios.example_english: The thief steals the wealth for himself.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'hṛñ' is listed under Bhvadi with the sense 'haraṇe' (taking away, removing, seizing). Marked with 'ñ', it is anit and ubhayapadi. In Sarvadhatuka tenses, Guna takes place on the vowel 'ṛ' yielding 'ar', producing 'harati' and 'harate'. With various prefixes such as pra, apa, vi, and a, the root exhibits diverse derived meanings.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'hṛñ haraṇe' as the act of carrying away or dispossessing. Being anit and ñit, it takes both padas depending on the recipient of the fruit of the action. Its nominal derivatives like hāra, haraṇa, and harita are derived systematically via kṛt affixes.

meanings.English: to carry, take away, steal, remove
meanings.Bengali: harana kara, churi kara, niye jaoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'maci' (appearing as 'manc') means to hold, support, raise, or uplift. In active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent physically or figuratively holding up or elevating an object. When made causative, it indicates causing someone or something to be raised or sustained.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present Tense (Lat)
scenarios.example_english: The pillar supports the building.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic), Present Tense (Lat)
scenarios.example_english: The artisan causes the stone to be raised.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'maci' is listed in the Bhvadi-gana with the meaning 'dharanocchrayayoh' (holding and elevating/raising). Because it is marked with the 'i' as an it-marker (idit), it receives a penultimate nasal infix (num-agama), yielding forms like 'mancati'. It takes Parasmaipada terminations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'maci dharanocchrayayoh' signifies both sustaining (dharana) and raising upwards (ucchraya). The idit condition accounts for the nasalization throughout conjugational paradigms.

meanings.English: to hold, to sustain, to raise, to uplift

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kuj' means to steal, rob, or take away covertly. It is conjugated in Parasmaipada in the Bhvadi Gana. When an agent acts directly to steal, standard active forms like 'kojati' are used. When someone causes another to commit theft, the causative affix (nic) is added to form 'kojayati' (causes to steal).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The thief steals the wealth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga (active voice), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The gang leader makes the servant steal the money.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kuja stene' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is marked for the sense of theft (stenatva/steya). Taking Guna of the root vowel 'u' to 'o' before Sarvadhatuka affixes like Shap, it forms 'kojati'. It takes the augment it in Ardhadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kuja stene' as denoting the act of theft or stealing. The derivation yields 'kojati, cukoja, kojita', highlighting its standard Parasmaipada inflection and vocalic strength under Guna.

meanings.English: to steal, to rob, to commit theft

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'chad' means to cover, conceal, or protect something with a cover or veil. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject performs the action of covering an external object. When combined with prefixes like 'a-', it means to wrap, clothe, or envelope.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi-gana Lat-lakara (Present Tense), Prathama-purusha (Third Person), Bahuvacana (Plural)
scenarios.example_english: The clouds cover the sun.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Prefix 'a' + Lat-lakara (Present Tense), Prathama-purusha (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The mother covers the child with a cloth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Under 'chada samvarane', Sayana notes that the root denotes the act of enclosing, covering, or concealing. It readily admits the causative and svarthe nic formations, exhibiting forms like chadayati and yielding derived nouns such as chadih and chada.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'samvarana' as the shielding or concealment of a substance from view. He illustrates the phonological conditioning and standard affixal derivation, emphasizing its core function of forming coverings and shelters.

meanings.English: To cover, conceal, shield, or wrap
meanings.Bengali: Dhaka dewa, aabrita kara, gopana kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jambh' (or 'jabh') means to stretch oneself, yawn, or expand limbs (gatravinama). It belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvadi-gana) and takes Atmanepada suffixes (like -te, -nte). Because it has a hidden 'i' marker (idit), an internal nasal 'm' appears in its standard forms, giving 'jambhate'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana (3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: Tired with sleepiness, the child stretches and yawns.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lan lakara (past tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Waking up in the morning, the infant stretched his limbs.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'jabhi gatraviname' is idit (marked with an 'i' indicatory letter), which necessitates the insertion of num-agama (a nasal sound) resulting in the base 'jambh'. Being anudattet, it takes Atmanepada endings in kartari prayoga yielding forms such as 'jambhate', 'jajambhe', and 'jambhitam'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'jabhi' signifies the stretching, contortion, or spreading of the limbs (gatravinamana/jrimbhana). Due to its idit nature, the penultimate nasal is constant across sarvadhatuka and ardhadhatuka environments, forming 'jambhate'.

meanings.English: to stretch limbs, yawn, gape, or expand
meanings.Kannada: deha hididu meredu muttuvudu, aakoluvudu, mai muriyuvudu
meanings.Hindi: angadaai lena, jamhaai lena, shareer phailana
meanings.Bengali: aangamora bhanga, hikka ba jrimbhan, gaa moshdaano

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ras' primarily means to taste, savor, relish, or show affection. In the basic active voice (Kartari Prayoga / Parasmaipada), it describes a subject experiencing or appreciating the flavor of food or an aesthetic sentiment. When used with causative markers (Nic), it shifts to 'making someone taste' or 'flavoring/seasoning' something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi-gana regular active present (Lat, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The child tastes and relishes the sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) present form
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the infant to taste the medicine.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'rasa asvadane' is listed in the Bhvadi class. It denotes the sensory action of tasting (asvadana) as well as showing affection or pleasure (sneha). Being an inherently Set root, it takes the intermediate 'i' augment across non-sarvadhatuka affixes (e.g., rarisitha, rasitum).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'rasa asvade', indicating the apprehension of sapidity or flavor. Derived nouns such as 'rasa' (juice, essence, taste, sentiment) trace directly from this verbal action.

meanings.English: To taste, relish, savor, appreciate flavor, or love

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'ghuṣ' means to make a loud sound, shout, or proclaim publicly. In basic form (Kartari Prayoga), the subject is doing the proclaiming directly. When causative suffix 'ṇic' is added, it means causing an announcement to be made or playing an instrument loudly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative 3rd person singular, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The king proclaims the royal order in the assembly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (Nic-pratyaya, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The servant beats the drum loudly in the city to announce the message.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ghuṣi~r' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with the it-marker 'ir', which leads to optional anit-status in the aorist (Luṅ) by the rule 'irito vā'. The primary meaning is 'viśabdana' denoting loud, distinct sounding or public declaration.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'viśabdana' as the distinct utterance of sound or proclamation. He notes the morphological variations where past passive participles take forms like 'ghuṣṭa' and 'ghoṣita' depending on technical semantic conditions (e.g., whether meaning loud sound or proclamation).

meanings.English: to proclaim, to make a loud sound, to announce
meanings.Bengali: ghoṣoṇā korā, citkār korā, śobdo korā
meanings.French: proclamer, crier hautement, faire du bruit
meanings.Chinese: xuan bu, da sheng jiao han, sheng ming

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root jñā in the Bhvadi gana specifically conveys three nuanced meanings: killing/injuring (marana), pleasing/satisfying (toshana), and perceiving or hearing/making sharp (nishamana). When used in standard active voice or causative constructions with mit-samjna rules (where the penultimate vowel shortens to 'a'), its meaning transforms distinctly between giving satisfaction and causing to perceive.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) with mit-samjna and vowel shortening (hrasva)
scenarios.example_english: The teacher pleases / informs the student.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) without vowel shortening (in the sense of killing/slaying)
scenarios.example_english: The hero slays the enemy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti clarifies that the root jñā is listed in the sense of marana (violence/killing), toshana (gratification/pleasing), and nishamana (perception/hearing). When taking the causative suffix Nic, the rule 'jna-marana-toshana-nishamaneshu' governs the application or non-application of mit-karya (shortening of the root vowel 'a' to 'a'), depending on whether destruction or cognition/satisfaction is intended.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that while jñā is widely recognized in Kryadi gana for general cognition (avabodhana), its occurrence in Bhvadi gana specifically addresses technical nuances of infliction (marana), delighting (toshana), and focused observation or making aware (nishamana).

meanings.English: to slay, to satisfy, to make perceive
meanings.Hindi: vadh karna, prasanna karna, jnana karana
meanings.Bengali: bodh kora, tushta kora, janiyan deoya
meanings.Chinese: sha si, shi man zu, shi zhi dao

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tras' means to be agitated, to fear, or to tremble. In its basic active voice (kartari prayoga), the subject feels fear or anxiety. By adding the causative suffix (ṇic), it shifts to 'trāsayati', meaning to scare, alarm, or frighten another person or animal.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana (optionally takes śap or śyan)
scenarios.example_english: The deer fears the lion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), laṭ-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The lion frightens the deer.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: trasī udvege - udvego bhayaṃ calanaṃ vā. 'vā bhrāśābhlaśobhramukramuklamatrasitruṭilaṣām' iti vikalpena śyan pratyayaḥ. trasati, trasyati; tatrāsa, trāsitaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: trasī udvege. udvegaścalanaṃ bhayaṃ ca. śyani kṛte trasyati, śapi trasati. setkāt trāsayati iti ṇau rūpam.

meanings.English: to fear, to tremble, to be agitated

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mrad' means to crush, grind, pound, or soften by pressing. It belongs to the first conjugation group (Bhvadi gana) and takes Atmanepada endings in its basic form (mradate). When converted into a causative (nic), it takes the form mradayati or mradayate to denote causing something to be crushed or softened.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer crushes the grain with his foot.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to be crushed / causes to soften
scenarios.example_english: The physician makes the student grind the medicine.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The author notes 'mrada mardane' as an Atmanepadi root of the Bhvadi gana. It takes the intermediate vowel 'i' (it) before ardhadhatuka affixes, forming mamrade in liti and mradita in luti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'mrada mardane' among roots signifying physical pressing, pulverizing, or reducing to a soft state, retaining its standard anudattet Atmanepada characteristics.

meanings.English: to crush, to pound, to trample, to grind, to soften
meanings.Bengali: churna kora, pesha, dolon kora, mordon kora
meanings.Chinese: nian sui, ya sui, rou mo

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tarj' expresses the action of scolding, rebuking, or threatening someone. In the standard active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject performs the act of censuring or intimidating another directly using basic primary suffixes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat-lakara (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The father reprimands the untruthful son.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lan-lakara (Past Imperfect), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The master scolded the wicked servant.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: tarja bhartsane. Bhartsanam santrasanam krodhena bhashanam ca. Iditvabhavat na num. Tarjati, tatarja, tarjita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: tarja bhartsane. Tarjanam krodhoktih santrasanam ca. Sakarmakah. Tarjati, atarjit.

meanings.English: To threaten, to scold, to censure, to reprimand
meanings.Bengali: Dhomkano, tarjon kora, bhiti prodorshon kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'san' means to serve, honour, obtain, or distribute. In normal active usage (Kartari Parasmaipada), the agent performs an act of serving, obtaining, or bestowing. When converted to the causative (Nic), it means to cause someone to receive, distribute, or bestow upon.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The devotee obtains merit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the wise man to receive wealth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'sana sambhaktau' belongs to Bhvadi gana. Initial dental 's' is derived from aupadeshika murdhanya 'sh' via dhatvadeh sah sah. In the simple active present tense it takes Shap pratyaya yielding sanati. In lit-lakara reduplication it forms sasana.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes sana sambhaktau as denoting both honouring/serving and sharing/obtaining. The vowel remains unlengthened before Sarvadhatuka affixes, forming sanati, sanatah, sananti.

meanings.English: to serve, to obtain, to honour, to share
meanings.Bengali: seba kara, prapto howa, bhajan kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'las' fundamentally describes shining, flashing, sparkling, or playfully moving/sporting. In simple active present tense (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings to form 'lasati' (shines or frolics). When the causative suffix (Nic) is added, it becomes 'lāsayati', meaning to cause someone or something to dance, sway, or radiate playfully.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Lightning flashes in the midst of clouds.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to sway / causes to dance
scenarios.example_english: The gentle breeze causes the tips of the creepers to dance.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya classifies 'lasa' in the sphere of brightness, radiance, and sport (kāntau krīḍāyāṃ ca). It is characterized as a Parasmaipada root with the augment 'iṭ' (seṭ), producing forms like lasati, lalāsa, lasitā, and lasiṣyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes the nuances of sporting, gleaming, and embracing (ślaiṣya/śleṣaṇa and krīḍana). In natural usage, it frequently compounds with upasargas such as 'ut' (ullasati - radiates or leaps with joy) and 'vi' (vilasati - gleams brightly or frolics).

meanings.English: To shine, flash, sparkle, play, sport, embrace
meanings.Hindi: Chamakna, shobha pana, khelna, kridan karna
meanings.Bengali: Jholmol kora, chomorano, khela kora, alingon kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'makṣ' means to collect, assemble, or bring things into a group. In regular active voice (Parasmaipada), it expresses the direct act of gathering or grouping objects together. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it means to cause someone or something to assemble or accumulate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The forest dweller gathers fruits in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (prayojaka kartari / nic pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The commander causes the soldiers to assemble at the post.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: makṣa sanghate. sanghata eka-sthanikarana-rupah samuhah. udattah parasmaipadisedhanukarah set. makṣati, mamakṣa, makṣita, makṣisyati ityadi rupani siddhyanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: makṣa sanghate. sanghatah samuccayah rasikaranam va. murdhanyantah set parasmaipadi. makṣati, makṣitavyam.

meanings.English: to collect, to gather, to assemble, to accumulate
meanings.Hindi: ikattha karna, bheed lagana, ekatra karna
meanings.Bengali: ekatra kara, sangraha kara, jamo kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tyaj' belongs to the 1st conjugation class (Bhvadi) and is used in the Parasmaipada voice to mean 'to leave', 'to abandon', or 'to give up'. When an affix for causation (Nic) is added, it forms 'tyājayati', meaning 'causes someone to give up or abandon'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The virtuous person abandons untruth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to give up or abandon
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the child to give up bad habits.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: tyaja hanau. hanir varjanam parityago va. sakarmakah parasmaibhashi anit ca. tyajati, tatyaja, tyakshyate ityadi rupany asya bhavanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: tyaja hanau. hanam parityagah upekshanam va. tyajati, tatyaja, tyakshyati, tyaktum. anid ayam.

meanings.English: to leave, to abandon, to renounce, to forsake

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'trauk' belongs to the Bhvadi class and means 'to go' or 'to move'. It always takes Atmanepada endings in its basic form because of its anudatta marker (traukate). When we want to express that someone makes another person move or approach, we add the causative suffix (Nic), turning it into 'traukayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana (kartari ātmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The young boy moves toward the village.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), laṭ-lakāra, parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The father causes the boy to go to school.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: traukṝ gatau. anudāttetvād ātmanepada-bhāk. seṭ. traukate, tutrauke, traokitā, traokiṣyate. gatyarthatvāt karmaṇi akarmakatvam api vivakṣyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: traukṝ gatau. ātmanepadī. traukate. aukāropadhaḥ. ṛkāra it.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to proceed
meanings.Chinese: xing jin, qian wang, yi dong

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mī' means to injure, hurt, or destroy. Because of the marker tag 'ṅ' in its original listing (mīṅ), it takes Ātmanepada endings in standard active voice. When conjugated in the present tense, its vowel 'ī' undergoes guṇa to 'e' and becomes 'ay' before vowel endings, producing forms like 'mayate' (he/she injures or destroys).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), laṭ lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Unrighteousness, being the cause of misery, destroys.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to destroy or causes to be injured
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the enemies to be destroyed through the soldier.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mīṅ hiṃsāyām. ṅitvād ātmanepadam. anudāttatvād aniṭ. sarvadhātuke guṇe 'y-ādeśe ca mayate iti rūpaṃ bhavati. liṭi mimye. luti mātā. lṛṭi māsyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mīṅ hiṃsāyām. ātmanepadī, anit. mayate, mimye, mātā, māsyate, amāsta. hiṃsā-karma-yoge sakarmakaḥ.

meanings.English: to injure, to hurt, to destroy, to kill
meanings.Bengali: himsa kora, binash kora, bodh kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klam' means to become tired, fatigued, or exhausted. In the basic present tense, the vowel lengthens to form 'klāmyati' (or 'klamati'), indicating someone getting weary on their own. When used with the causative affix (ṇic), it forms 'klamayati', meaning to cause someone else to get exhausted or to tire someone out.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice, present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: After walking a lot on the road, the traveler becomes fatigued.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya, active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The intense heat exhausts the farmer.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'klamu glānau' belongs to the Bhvādi class. Under the rule 'śamāṁ aṣṭānāṁ dīrghaḥ śyani', the penultimate vowel undergoes lengthening in the presence of the Śyan pratyaya, producing 'klāmyati'. As an aniṭ root, in the past passive participle (niṣṭhā), it drops its nasal and takes lengthening under relevant sutras to form 'klāntaḥ'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'glāni' as physical looseness or weariness (śarīra-śaithilyam). He details the derivation of forms like 'klāmyati' alongside the standard Bhvādi 'klamati', noting the morphophonemic treatment in kṛt affixes such as 'klāntaḥ' without the intermediate iṭ augment.

meanings.English: To be fatigued, to become exhausted, to languish, to tire
meanings.Bengali: Klanto howa, parishranto howa, abashanna howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'lañj' means to reproach, blame, or scold someone. It is used in the active voice (Parasmaipada) taking regular Bhvadi present-tense endings like '-ati' with an internal nasal marker from its idit character (forming 'lañjati'). When modified with causative affixes, it conveys causing or directing someone to reproach another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher scolds the negligent student.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to be scolded or reprimanded.
scenarios.example_english: The manager causes the offending employee to be reprimanded.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti defines 'lañji' in the sense of 'bhartsana' (scolding, reproaching, or threatening). Due to being marked with 'i' (idit), it takes an invariant penultimate nasal (num-agama), deriving forms such as 'lañjati', 'lalañja', and 'lañjitā'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'lañji bhartsane' that the root conveys the meaning of blaming or censuring ('nindā' or 'bhartsana'). The internal nasal remains constant across non-conjugational stems as well, operating as a standard Set Parasmaipada root.

meanings.English: to scold, reproach, blame, or censure
meanings.Bengali: tiroskar kora, bhortsona kora, dosh dewa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vel' fundamentally means to move, sway, or tremble. In standard Kartari Parasmaipada, it describes a subject moving or waving naturally. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it shifts the meaning to actively shaking, swinging, or rocking an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative active, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The branch of the tree sways due to the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The mother rocks the baby in the cradle.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: velr calane. velati, vivela, velita. calanam kampa iti vyakhyatam. nic-pratyaye velayati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: velr calane. calane ityarthah. velati. khel-vel-adayo gatyartha api bhavantity eke.

meanings.English: to move, sway, shake, tremble

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhrāṅś' means to shine, gleam, or emit radiant light. It is an Atmanepada root. Under Paninian rules, it can optionally take the Shyan affix in the present tense, giving two valid forms: 'bhrāṅśate' and 'bhrāṅśyate'. In the causative form (Nic), it changes to Parasmaipada/Ubhayapada as 'bhrāṅśayati', meaning 'to illuminate' or 'to make something shine'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (optional Shyan pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The star shines brightly in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The lamp illuminates the room.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'bhrāṅśṛ' is listed in the sense of 'dīptau' (shining/radiating). The letter 'ṛ' is an it-marker. Being anudattet, it receives Atmanepada terminations. By the rule 'vā bhrāśabhlaśabhramu...' (Panini 3.1.70), the vikarana Shyan is optionally applied in the active voice, yielding both 'bhrāṅśate' and 'bhrāṅśyate'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'bhrāṅśṛ dīptau' as prakashe (radiance or illumination). It is grouped with roots like bhrāś, bhlāś, and bhlāmś, noting its optional Shyan-vikarana forms alongside standard Shap forms.

meanings.English: to shine, to gleam, to radiate light, to be luminous
meanings.Bengali: jholmol kora, ujjval howa, dipti pawa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'murch' (often written as mūrch) primarily means to faint or lose consciousness, and secondarily to expand, swell, or solidify. In ordinary active voice (Parasmaipada), it shows someone fainting or a quality/sound swelling. When used with causative affixes (Nic), it changes from intransitive to transitive, meaning to stupefy, enchant, or make someone faint.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (Laṭ), 3rd person singular, Kartari Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: Due to the intense heat, the traveler faints on the road.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative present tense (Ṇijanta Laṭ), Kartari Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The divine celestial melody enchants and overwhelms everyone.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'murchā' belongs to the Bhvādi class and has the twin senses of 'moha' (loss of sensory awareness or consciousness) and 'samucchraya' (swelling, elevation, or solidification into a dense state). The root forms present-stem 'mūrccha-' via standard ch-gemination rules yielding 'mūrcchati'. In the past passive participle, it forms 'mūrchita' or 'mūrcchita'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'mohaḥ sañjñānāśaḥ' (fainting is cessation of cognitive awareness) and 'samucchrayaḥ saṅghātaḥ pravṛddhiśca' (gathering mass, thickening, or intensifying). The root is listed as Parasmaipadi and Set.

meanings.English: to faint, swoon, lose consciousness, solidify, swell
meanings.Hindi: mūrcchit honā, behōś honā, baḍhanā, jamnā
meanings.Bengali: mūrcchita haoyā, jñāna hārānō, bṛddhi pāoyā
meanings.German: ohnmächtig werden, das Bewusstsein verlieren, anschwellen
meanings.Russian: padat v obmorok, teryat soznaniye, sgushchatsya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kr' (kṝ) belongs to the 1st conjugation class and means 'to harm, injure, or hurt'. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), the agent performs the act of hurting someone or something. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it signifies making someone cause harm or inflicting damage through an intermediary.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person harms the righteous person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: He/she causes (someone) to harm or inflict injury.
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the servant to injure the enemy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṝ' is listed in the Bhvadi-gana with the semantic marker 'himsayam' (in the sense of harming, injuring, or destroying). In the universal Sarvadhatuka system with Shap-pratyaya, guna applies to the vowel yielding 'ar', thus forming the present stem 'kara-' and the primary finite form 'karati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'kṝ himsayam' among the r-ending roots of the first group. It expresses injury or inflicting violence. It is Anit in the primary non-periphrastic systems, taking regular guna transformations before vocalic Sarvadhatuka affixes.

meanings.English: to injure, harm, hurt, or destroy
meanings.Hindi: himsa karna, chot pahunchana, dukh dena
meanings.Bengali: himsa kora, aghat kora, khoti kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root liś primarily expresses the action of going, moving, or diminishing in size. In basic active voice (Kartari Parasmaipada), it simply means someone or something moves or travels. When we attach the causative suffix (Nic), it changes to mean causing someone to move or reducing/lessening something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present active 3rd person singular with Sap)
scenarios.example_english: The guide goes along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative active 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to move / directs to go
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd makes the cows move towards the forest.
