When used with the causative suffix (Nic), the meaning shifts to making something else rustle, vibrate, or grow dense.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple present tense (Lat lakara, kartari prayoga, prathama-purusha ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: Rustles or makes a low sound
scenarios.example_english: In the forest, the leaf rustles due to the breezes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative present tense (Nic pratyaya, kartari prayoga, prathama-purusha ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The wind softly makes the creepers rustle.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kuñja śabde balībhāve ca. kuñjati, kukoñja, kuñjitā. balībhāvaḥ samāhatiḥ stambho vā. seṭ parasmaipadī.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kuñja śabde balībhāve ca. śabdo'tra dhvaniviśeṣaḥ. balībhāvaḥ stambhaḥ. kuñjati. nikuñjaḥ iti vihārasthānam.

meanings.English: To make a rustling sound, to murmur, to be dense or thick
meanings.Kannada: Shabda maduvudu, nikuñjada roopadalli bariyuvudu, dattavaguvudu
meanings.Tamil: Oli seithal, adarthiyathal, sadasada oli ezhupputhal
meanings.Hindi: Dhvani ya sarasarahata paida karna, ghana hona
meanings.Bengali: Shabdo kora ba jhonkar toiri kora, ghono howa
meanings.German: Rascheln, ein leises Geraeusch machen, dicht werden
meanings.French: Bruire, emettre un froissement, devenir touffu

canonical_dhatvartha: gati-pujanayoh (in the sense of movement, bending, or worship/honoring)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'añc' expresses moving, bending, reaching towards, or honoring/worshiping someone. In active present tense (Parasmaipada), it forms 'añcati'. When a causative suffix (Nic) is added, it forms 'añcayati', meaning to cause to bend or to direct/illuminate something towards someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Lat Lakara (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The devotee honors (or turns towards) the deity.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara
scenarios.meaning: causes to move, bends, or makes manifest
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the student to embrace (turn towards) the truth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'añcu~' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana and is classified with the meaning of 'gati' (movement/turning) and 'pūjana' (honoring/reverence). In standard classical usage, it takes the 'śap' vikarana and retains the nasal in strong environments, yielding forms such as añcati and añcataḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'añcu~' denotes motion and worshipful bending. When compounded with upasargas (like ud-añc, pra-añc, sam-añc), it denotes distinct physical directions, spatial orientations, and manifestations of honor.

meanings.English: to move, bend, reach towards, honor, or worship

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'kūj' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvādi gaṇa) and primarily means to make an inarticulate, soft, or melodious sound, such as the chirping of birds or the cooing of cuckoos. In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes the natural singing or sound produced by birds and insects. In the causative form, it signifies causing something to hum, resound, or make sounds.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha (3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The cuckoo coos sweetly on the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative stem), Lat lakara (present tense)
scenarios.meaning: causes to resound or makes chirp
scenarios.example_english: The spring season makes the birds chirp in the forest.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kūja avyakte śabde. bhvādiḥ parasmaipadī seṭ. dhātorguṇābhāvaḥ dirghopadhatvāt. kūjati, cakūja, kūjitā, kūjiṣyati, akūjīt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kūja śabde. avyakto madhuraśca pakṣyādiravaḥ. udāharaṇam - kūjati kokilagaṇaḥ.

meanings.English: to coo, chirp, warble, make an inarticulate sound
meanings.Bengali: kūjana karā, pākhira ḍākā, kalaraba karā

canonical_dhatvartha: bandhane granthane ca (in the sense of binding, stringing together, or composing)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root drbh means to string together, arrange, or bind. In its basic Atmanepada form (drembhate), the subject performs the act of stringing or weaving items together. When converted to the causative form (drembhayati or darbhayati), it denotes making someone else arrange or compose items into an orderly series.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The garland-maker strings flowers together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to string or arrange together
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the student to compose the work.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that the root dṛbhi belongs to the bhvadi-gana with the idit marker which induces a penultimate nasal (num-agama), yielding forms like drembhate. The core semantic sphere is established as bandhana (binding) and granthana (stringing together or composing sequentially).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin identifies dṛbhi as an idit root denoting granthana (weaving/interlacing) and samghata (assembling). The canonical present tense formation proceeds with guna of the vowel followed by nasalization due to the it-marker, producing drembhate.

meanings.English: to string together, weave, bind, compose

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ras' fundamentally means to taste, savor, or relish flavors. In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), the subject experiences or tastes food or drink. When used in causative constructions, it implies causing someone to taste or flavoring something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present Active indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The child tastes the sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative / Nic pratyaya (Present Active indicative)
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the child taste the milk.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya explains the root 'rasa asvadane' as the direct sensory engagement of tasting (rasanam) and relishing the essence of culinary or experiential objects. It takes standard Bhvadi vikarana sap, operating as set and parasmaipadi to yield forms like rasati and arasit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'rasa' in the sense of 'asvadane' (experiencing flavor) as well as producing sound in certain contextual usages. The primary derivation proceeds with regular guna and set inflection across universal conjugations.

meanings.English: to taste, to relish, to savor

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root rās means to make a sound, howl, bray, or cry out. In its regular active usage, it takes Atmanepada endings. When expressing causative action (making someone or something produce a sound), it takes the nic-pratyaya and conjugates in Parasmaipada.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The donkey brays loudly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to make a sound / provokes to cry out
scenarios.example_english: The boy causes the animal to cry out with a stick.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: rāsa shabde. anudātteccātmanepadam. rāsate, rerāsyate, rāsayate. aniṭ-lakṣaṇam arāsta iti rāddham.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: rāsa shabde. ātmanepada-prayogaḥ. rāsate gardabha iti dhvanikaraṇārthe prayujyate.

meanings.English: to sound, to cry out, to bray, to howl
meanings.Tamil: oli ezhuppu, kattuthal, kazhuthai pola kattu
meanings.German: schreien, brullen, laute von sich geben

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sphul' means to blossom, open up, or expand like a budding flower. Because it is in the active voice (Parasmaipada), it simply describes a subject expanding or bursting into bloom on its own. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it means to cause something to blossom or open up.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The flower blossoms in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya), Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The sunlight causes the bud to blossom.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'sphula vikacane' as expanding or blooming open (praphullibhavana). Being an udattetta root, it takes Parasmaipada affixes and admits the intermediate 'i' augment (it-agama) in non-sarvadhatuka positions, yielding present forms such as spholati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'sphula vikacane' shares close semantic affinity with sphuṭa and sphura, indicating manifestation, opening forth, or bursting into view with guna strengthening of the vowel 'u' to 'o' before sarvadhatuka affixes.

meanings.English: to blossom, expand, open up, burst forth

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'mluc' fundamentally means to go, move, or recede/set (like the sun or celestial bodies). In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject moving or descending. When paired with upasargas (prefixes) like 'apa' or 'abhy-upa', it specifies moving away or setting/disappearing.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense, 3rd person singular, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The sun goes down / sets upon the setting mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'apa' prefixation in Kartari Prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The deer slips away into the forest.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mlucu' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana with the sense 'gatau' (to move, go). It takes Shap pratyaya, undergoes guna of the penultimate vowel 'u' to 'o' yielding 'mlocati'. It is anit in standard past formations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mlucu gatau' along with 'mrucu gatau' as synonyms denoting motion, particularly slow or descending movement, forming the primary finite form 'mlocati'.

meanings.English: To go, move, slip away, or set (as of the sun)
meanings.Hindi: Jana, chalna, ast hona ya chhipna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kāś' means to shine, appear bright, or be visible. By default, it takes Atmanepada endings in the active voice. When combined with prefixes like 'pra' or used with the causative affix (nic), it extends its meaning to illuminating or revealing something to others.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi First Person / Kartari Atmanepada Lat Lakara
scenarios.example_english: The moon shines brightly in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (Nic-pratyaya) with prefix 'pra'
scenarios.example_english: The lamp illuminates the entire house.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kāśṛ dīptau. dīptih prakāśanam. anudātta itvadātmanepadam. kāśate, cakāśe, kāśitā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kāśṛ dīptau. dīptiprakāśayoh. kāśate, cakāśe. upasargayogāt prakāśe nirdiṣṭam.

meanings.English: to shine, to look bright, to appear, to radiate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gṝ' primarily means to make sound, praise, or utter, and in related usages, to swallow or invoke. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it typically forms 'girati' or 'garati' to denote vocalizing, uttering words, or addressing someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi/Tudadivat Parasmaipada Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The poet utters a verse.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the student to recite the hymn.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root gṝ is listed under śabdārtha (to make a sound, utter, or praise). In certain contexts and conjugational forms, it undergoes riṅ-ādeśa yielding forms like girati, retaining the sense of vocalization and utterance.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes gṝ as śabdakarma, forming girati or garati in the present tense, distinguishing its semantic scope of vocal sound and speech from roots indicating mere noise.

meanings.English: to utter, sound, recite, or call

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhaṭ' primarily means to nourish, maintain, or serve for wages/hire (bhṛti). In the regular active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an individual working for wages or maintaining someone. In the causative form (ṇijanta), it conveys employing someone or providing maintenance/wages.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present active indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: works for wages / earns maintenance / serves
scenarios.example_english: The servant serves in the master's house for wages.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative present active indicative)
scenarios.meaning: hires someone / pays wages to maintain
scenarios.example_english: The king employs and maintains the warriors with wages.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root bhaṭa is given in the sense of bhṛtau (bhṛtiḥ vetanādānam - receiving wages or providing livelihood). As a standard Bhvādi Parasmaipada root with a penultimate short vowel, it forms bhaṭati in laṭ, babhāṭa in liṭ, and bhaṭitā in luṭ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines bhaṭa in the sense of bhṛti (wages/livelihood), noting the derivation of nominal forms like 'bhaṭaḥ' (a hired soldier or bodyguard supported by regular payment).

meanings.English: to hire, to maintain, to nourish, to serve for wages
meanings.Kannada: vetana nīḍi poṣisuvudu, bhatyavannu koṭṭu iḍisikoḷḷuvudu
meanings.Tamil: vētaṉam koṭuttu vaḷarttal, sambalam koṭuttu paṇikkamarttutal
meanings.Malayalam: vētaṉam nalki pōṣippikkuka, śambaḷam nalki panikku vekkuka
meanings.Hindi: vetana dekar poṣaṇa karanā, vetana para rakhanā
meanings.Bengali: betana diye rākhā bā poṣaṇa karā
meanings.Russian: nanimat za platu, soderzhat, vyplachivat zhalovane

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣlep' conveys the state of dejection, wretchedness, or feeling downcast and miserable. As an inherently Ātmanepada verb in the Bhvādi class, it conjugates using middle-voice endings (e.g., kṣlepate). When causatives (ṇic) are added, it means causing someone to become dejected or bringing someone to distress.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakāra (present tense), prathama-puruṣa (3rd person), ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Becomes dejected, suffers wretchedness, or feels miserable
scenarios.example_english: The traveler in the forest suffers wretchedly due to hunger.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇijanta), Parasmaipada, Lat-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes dejection or brings someone to distress
scenarios.example_english: Poverty depresses and causes misery to people.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṣlepṛ' is listed with the meaning 'dainye' (wretchedness, dejection, or depression). The final 'ṛ' is an it-marker to prevent lengthening under certain conditions. It belongs to the Bhvādi class and takes Ātmanepada terminations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses 'kṣlepṛ dainye' along with related roots like glep and klep, noting its usage in denoting miserable or depressed physical and emotional states.

meanings.English: to be wretched, to be dejected, to suffer misery

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sal' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and takes Parasmaipada endings. It primarily denotes moving, flowing, or gentle shaking. In the causative (nic) form, it expresses causing someone or something to move or stir.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present tense, active voice, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: When the wind blows, the leaf moves.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative active, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The wind causes the branch of the tree to move.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'ṣala' belongs to the Bhvadi class, having the initial dental replacement from dental/retroflex sibilant 'ṣa' to 'sa' by 'dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ'. It takes 'sap' vikarana and expresses movement (gati) and agitation (calana).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini classifies 'ṣala gatau' among the roots signifying motion and shaking, conjugate in Parasmaipada without thematic irregularities (salati, sasāla, salitā).

meanings.English: to move, to tremble, to stir

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root dhauk inherently means to move, approach, or advance toward someone or something. In standard Sanskrit, it operates in the Atmanepada voice (dhaukate). When modified by prefixes like upa- or converted to the causative form (dhaukayati), it often conveys the sense of bringing forward or presenting an offering.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves toward the water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga upa + causative affix (Nic) in Kartari prayoga
scenarios.meaning: presents or offers as a gift
scenarios.example_english: The devotee presents a fruit to the deity.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti lists dhauki under the heading of roots signifying motion (gatau). It confirms its identity as an Atmanepadi root with the addition of the intermediate vowel i (set), yielding the standard present tense base dhaukate and the reduplicated perfect dudhauke.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines dhauki as denoting physical displacement or directed approach (gatyarthah). He details its morphological evolution in non-conjugational tenses, highlighting that forms such as dhaukita and dudhauke follow regular vowel gradation and set-guna rules.

meanings.English: to approach, to move towards, to advance

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kluñc' means to bend, become crooked, or curve. In simple Parasmaipada form, it describes a subject naturally curling, bending, or curving. When the causative suffix (Nic) is added, it turns into an active action meaning to cause something to bend or make something crooked.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The old man's walking stick bends.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to bend or makes something crooked
scenarios.example_english: The blacksmith bends the iron rod.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti lists this root under the Bhvadi class with the sense 'kuṭībhāva' (curvature, bending, shrinking). As an un-accented ending root, it takes Parasmaipada terminations yielding forms like kluñcati in present tense and cukloñca in the perfect tense.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes the roots kruñca and kluñca jointly under 'kuṭībhāve', showing the phonetic alternation between 'r' and 'l' (ralayor abhedaḥ) to indicate bending, curving, or making irregular in form.

meanings.English: to bend, to curve, to shrink, to become crooked
meanings.German: sich biegen, sich krümmen, krumm werden

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root svad means to taste, savor, or to be delicious and pleasing to the palate. In its standard Atmanepada form (svadate), it describes tasting food or something being delightful to taste. When converted into a causative verb (svadayati), it means to make something savory, sweeten it, or serve someone delicious food.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice, present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy relishes the sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nich-pratyaya (causative present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The mother sweetens the kheer with sugar.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: svada asvadane. asvadanam rasanendriyena rasasya anubhavah. anudatteta atmanepadam. svadate, sasvade, svadita, svadishyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: svada asvadane. svadate. asvadanam rasagrahane madhuratve cha vartate. svadita, svadayate.

meanings.English: to taste, to relish, to savor, to be palatable
meanings.Bengali: svad grohon kora, asvadan kora, mishti laga
meanings.Russian: probovat na vkus, smakovát', byt' vkusnym

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'madi' contains an 'i' as an it-marker (idit), which causes a nasal 'n' to be inserted before the final consonant, transforming the base into 'mand-'. Operating in the Atmanepada, it expresses rejoicing, being delighted, or singing praise. When changed to the causative form with the affix 'nic', it means 'to gladden' or 'to cause someone to rejoice'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana (Present Tense, 3rd Person Singular, Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The devotee rejoices in or praises Lord Hari.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) with Parasmaipada in Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The good news gladdens the friend.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: madi stutimodamadanamasvitsveshu ityeke. idittvat num. mandate, mamande, mandita, mandishyate. stutau sakarmakah, harsha-glapana-svapneshv akarmakah. nic-sannanta-rupeshu num-anuvrittih siddhyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: madi harsha-stutyocete. idid ayam numam labhate. mandate harim devah, harshe tu svayam eva mandate iti bhedah.

meanings.English: to praise, to rejoice, to delight, to be glad
meanings.Hindi: stuti karna, prasanna hona, harshit hona
meanings.Bengali: stuti kora, anandita howa, ullasita howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mūtr' belongs to the Bhvādi class (adanta group) and signifies the physiological act of urinating or discharging fluid. In primary active usage, it takes Parasmaipada terminations. When used causatively, it indicates causing someone or an animal to discharge urine or pass water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present active 3rd person singular, adanta-lakṣaṇa / svārthe ṇic)
scenarios.example_english: The child urinates in sleep.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Ṇic prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the infant urinate.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mūtra' is read in the context of 'prasrāve' (discharging urine). Being an adanta (ending in short 'a') root in the Bhvādi collection, it regularly incorporates the affix forming forms like 'mūtrayati' or 'mūtrati' to denote biological excretion.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'mūtra prasrāve' as denoting the natural act of excretion and voiding liquid waste ('mūtrakriyāyām'). Forms derived exhibit regular vowel preservation and seṭ character.

meanings.English: to urinate, to discharge urine

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣap' means to send, cast, or spend/pass time. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject performs the act of casting or spending time. In causative constructions (Nic), it signifies making someone send or causing to pass/waste time.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga, Lat, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The sage spends time in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Lat, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to spend, wastes, or drives away
scenarios.example_sanskrit: saḥ vyarthena dhanaṁ kālaṁ ca kṣapayati.
scenarios.example_english: He wastes wealth and time uselessly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'kṣapa prerane' in the Bhvadi-gana. It is classified under the Parasmaipada paradigm taking the thematic 'sap' vikarana. Forms like kṣapati, cakṣāpa, kṣapitā are derived, retaining the sense of driving forward, motivating, or dispatching.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'kṣapa prerane' as denoting propulsion, casting, or the expenditure of time and effort. It takes standard Parasmaipada inflectional terminations in the Sarvadhatuka tenses with Guna/vowel preservation.

meanings.English: to send, to drive, to cast, to pass time
meanings.Bengali: prerana kara, samaya katano, kshepa kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'krap' means to feel pity, show compassion, or mourn/lament. Being fundamentally an Atmanepada root in the Bhvadi class, its action reflects the inner emotional disposition of the subject. When modified into the causative form (nic), it conveys causing someone to lament or arousing deep compassion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Present indicative active subject, Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The kind man feels pity for the poor boy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to lament / arouses compassion in
scenarios.example_english: His pitiful words arouse compassion in everyone's heart.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'krapa' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana and is categorized under 'kṛpāyām' meaning to experience pity, show mercy, or express grief. Being anudattet, it takes Atmanepada affixes in non-causative conjugations without intermediate augment (anit in basic forms).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'krapa kṛpāyām' as conveying both the sentiment of feeling compassion (daya) and vocalizing distress or sorrow (karunokti / vilapa), yielding forms such as krapate and cakrape.

meanings.English: to pity, to show compassion, to mourn, to lament
meanings.Hindi: daya karna, kripa karna, shok jatana
meanings.Bengali: doya kora, koruna kora, shok kora
meanings.French: avoir de la pitie, compatir, pleurer

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klam' means to become tired, weary, or exhausted. When used normally in active voice, it describes a person or living being naturally growing fatigued from effort. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it changes meaning to making someone or something tired.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice, present tense, Lat lakara with Syan/Shap modification)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler becomes tired from the journey.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Preranartha (Causative / Nic pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: Hard work exhausts the boy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: klamu glanau. Asya dhatu-patha-sthasya samjnayam dirgha-vidhana-bhedah. 'va samam astanam dirghah syan ca' iti sutrena klamyati klamati iti ubhayatha rupa-siddhih bhavati. Glanir nama sarirasya cetaso va saktihrasah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: klamu glanau. Glanir utsahahani-rupa. Syani dhyayaniti dirghah - klamyati, klamati. Anit-dhatuh.

meanings.English: to grow weary, to become fatigued, to languish, to tire
meanings.Bengali: klanto howa, obosonno howa, klanti anubhob kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'puṭ' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvādi-gaṇa) and signifies bringing together, connecting, or folding into layers (saṃsarga). In active voice (Kartari), it takes Parasmaipada terminations to describe joining or folding an object. When modified by the causative suffix (ṇic), it shifts to 'poṭayati', meaning to cause someone or something to connect, pack, or fold.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present tense), Prathama-puruṣa (3rd person), Eka-vacana, Kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The boy folds the paper for safekeeping.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Ṇijanta), Laṭ (Present tense), Prathama-puruṣa, Kartari prayoga
scenarios.meaning: Causes to fold or binds together
scenarios.example_english: The physician binds the medicine together with a cloth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'puṭa saṃsarge' is read in the Bhvādi-gaṇa. It denotes connection, intimate contact, or mutual association (saṃśleṣa). Being an udātta Parasmaipada root with a penultimate short vowel, it forms the present stem 'puṭati' with guṇa absent before śap due to lack of standard conditions, but undergoes guṇa in the causative formation 'poṭayati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin glosses 'puṭa saṃsarge' as expressing the act of bringing parts into contact, blending, or shaping into a concave layer or vessel (puṭīkaraṇa). It belongs to the set of unaccented Parasmaipada roots taking standard 'iṭ' augment in non-conjugational tenses.

meanings.English: to connect, to fold, to bring into contact, to unite
meanings.Bengali: jukto karā, saṃsparśe ānā, bhāṅj karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klam' means to become tired, weary, or exhausted. It takes an elongated vowel 'a' -> 'a' in its base present tense stem, appearing as 'klamati' (or 'klamyati'). In the causative form (Nic), it changes meaning to 'to tire out' or 'to cause someone to become fatigued'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present active 3rd person singular with vowel lengthening)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler gets exhausted after walking on the road.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) active voice
scenarios.example_english: The heavy burden exhausts the boy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'klamu glanau' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is categorized as Anit and Parasmaipadi. Madhava notes the application of elongation rules (sam-adi group behavior) yielding 'klamati' or 'klamyati', and details the forms in perfect (caklama) and aorist (aklamat).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'klamu' in the sense of 'glani' (physical loss of strength or mental weariness). He confirms its Anit nature and lists the phonological developments across principal tense stems.

meanings.English: to become weary, to feel fatigue, to exhaust

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hve' fundamentally means to call aloud, summon, invoke, or challenge to a contest. Because it is an Ubhayapada root (marked with the 'ñ' it-marker), it operates in both Parasmaipada and Atmanepada. Generally, Parasmaipada forms like 'hvayati' express standard summoning or calling out to another person. When expressing mutual rivalry, challenging an opponent (spardha), or when used with prefixes like 'a-', it frequently takes Atmanepada forms like 'āhvayate'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada, Lat lakara (present indicative)
scenarios.example_english: The father calls his son home.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Atmanepada with 'āṅ' prefix (denoting rivalry or inviting for oneself)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior challenges the opponent on the battlefield.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Sayana explains 'hveñ spardhāyāṁ viśabde ca' where spardhā denotes saṅgharṣa (competition or challenging) and viśabda denotes viśeṣataḥ śabdanam (summoning or calling aloud). Being ñ-it, it takes Parasmaipada or Atmanepada depending on the fruit of the action (svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale). In the present tense (śap), ay-ādeśa yields 'hvayati' and 'hvayate', while before kit/ṅit suffixes (like kta and liṭ), it undergoes samprasāraṇa into 'hū-' (e.g., hūtaḥ, juhāva, juhuve).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the root's dual semantics as 'saṅgharṣa' (mutual rivalry/defiance) and 'āhvāna' (calling near). He notes that the root possesses an anubandha 'ñ' which establishes its Ubhayapada nature, and outlines the morphophonemic alternation between the diphthong base and samprasarana contraction in passive and participial formations.

meanings.English: to call, summon, invoke, challenge

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tras' means to fear, tremble, or become anxious. In standard active usage (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject experiencing fear or shaking from distress. When used in the causative (Nic), it shifts the meaning to causing someone else to fear or frightening someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The deer is afraid of the lion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The lion terrifies the deer.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti specifies 'trasī udvege' in the Bhvadi-gana as taking the primary sense of udvega (agitation, fear, or trembling). It is an idit root due to the canonical marker, which leads to forms like trasati in the present tense, distinguishing its Bhvadi usage from its Divadi class counterpart.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'trasī udvege' that the root conveys mental agitation and fear. It operates with standard Parasmaipada inflection without Vikarana anomalies in the first class, yielding regular conjugational forms such as trasati, tatrasa, and trasishyati.

meanings.English: to tremble, to fear, to be agitated

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mruc' means to go, to move, or to set/decline (like a celestial body). It is used exclusively in Parasmaipada in the active voice. When forming the simple present tense, the vowel 'u' undergoes guna strengthening to 'o', yielding 'mrocati' (he/she goes or sets). In causative forms with the suffix nic, it means to cause to go or to lead away.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (kartari prayoga), Present tense (lat lakara), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The sun moves (sets) towards the mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative stem (nic pratyaya), Active voice, Present tense
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd causes the cow to move.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'mrucu gatau' as a motion-signifying root of the first conjugation (Bhvadi). Being Parasmaipadi, it forms the present base with sap and guna, resulting in 'mrocati'. Its perfect tense forms reduplicated stem 'mumroca', behaving similarly to other guttural-final motion verbs like mluc.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'mrucu' is classified under 'gatau' (movement/going). He specifies the regular guna progression in Sarvadhatuka environments ('mrocati') and notes its parallel usage with 'mlucu' in the sense of motion and going down or disappearing.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to set or sink

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'subh' primarily means to shine, glow, or look beautiful and elegant. It takes Atmanepada endings in its base form because of its anudatta marker. When used in the causative form (nic), it shifts to meaning 'to beautify' or 'to adorn', allowing both Padas.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (Base Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The moon looks splendid in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Parasmaipada, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Knowledge beautifies a person.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'subha diptau' is marked with anudatta indicator vowel, establishing it as an Atmanepadi root. In Sarvadhatuka environments, guna of the vowel 'u' takes place before the affix 'sap', yielding 'sobhate'. In Ardhadhatuka tenses, it takes the intermediate 'i' augment (set), producing forms like sobhita and asobhista.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'subha diptau' as having the primary sense of radiant illumination and graceful appearance (diptih sobha). The root undergoes standard vowel gradation to 'o' across gunavaha affixes and forms derived nouns like sobha and subha.

meanings.English: to shine, to look splendid, to be radiant
meanings.Bengali: shobha pawa, ujjvala howa, sundara dekhano

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'krath' belongs to the 1st class (Bhvadi) and means to hurt, injure, or kill. It takes Parasmaipada endings in normal active usage. When causative affixes (Nic) are added, it means to cause someone to injure or destroy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana, kartari prayoga (active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior strikes and injures the enemy in battle.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the enemies to be slain by the soldiers.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti defines 'kratha' under the meaning 'hiṁsāyām' (causing injury, striking, or killing). It is classified as an udātta, parasmaipadi, and seṭ root of the Bhvādi gaṇa, yielding forms like krathati, cakrātha, and krathitā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'kratha hiṁsāyām' emphasizing the sense of violent affliction, destruction, and killing, pointing out standard active paradigm forms such as krathati and krathitavān.

meanings.English: To kill, to injure, to strike, to destroy
meanings.Bengali: Hotya kora, aghat kora, binash kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khal' means to shake, move, or tremble. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an object or person moving or trembling on its own. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it shifts meaning to causing someone or something else to shake or move.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active indicative 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: When the wind blows, the tree branch shakes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya with Lat lakara)
scenarios.meaning: causes to shake or moves something
scenarios.example_english: The strong wind causes the tree to shake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'khala sañcalane' as a root belonging to the Bhvadi class taking Parasmaipada endings. As an it-bearing (Set) root, forms like cakhāla, khalitā, and khaliṣyati are derived in regular accordance with standard guna and augment rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses 'khala sañcalane' with 'calanam', signifying general trembling, agitation, or unsteady movement, forming khalati and its standard primary derivatives without irregular vriddhi.

meanings.English: to shake, to tremble, to move

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhukṣ' means to kindle, fan a fire, or revive energy and enthusiasm. It is commonly used in Atmanepada with the prefix 'sam' (sandhukṣate) to express rekindling or keeping a flame alive.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana, ātmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The gentle breeze rekindles the fire.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakāra, parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The teacher kindles enthusiasm in the students.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhukṣa~' is defined in the sense of 'sandīpana' (kindling, exciting, or blazing). Being anudāttet, it takes Ātmanepada terminations to form 'dhukṣate' and with prefix 'sam', 'sandhukṣate'. In lit-lakara it forms 'dudhukṣe'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'dhukṣa sandīpane' as illuminating, igniting, or animating, noting that the root frequently occurs in classical usage with the upasarga 'sam' to denote revitalizing or flaming up.

meanings.English: to kindle, to ignite, to fan a flame, to stimulate
meanings.Hindi: sulagana, prajvalita karana, bharakana, uttejita karana

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klīb' means to lack boldness, to behave timidly, or to lose heart/courage. It is naturally used in the Atmanepada voice to denote a person experiencing self-doubt or showing a lack of valor.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative, 3rd person singular, Atmanepada)
scenarios.meaning: Acts timidly / loses courage / behaves unmanly
scenarios.example_english: Seeing the enemy in battle, the cowardly person loses courage.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kta-pratyaya (Past passive participle acting as state predicate)
scenarios.example_english: Even in times of crisis, he did not become disheartened.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: klībṛ adhārṣṭye. dhārṣṭyaṃ pragalbhatā, tadabhāvo 'dhārṣṭyam kādaryam. ṛkāro 'nudanbandhaḥ 'anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam' ityetadarthaḥ. klībate, klībāñcakre, klībitā, klībiṣyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: klībṛ adhārṣṭye. dhṛṣṭasya bhāvaḥ dhārṣṭyaṃ pragalbhatā, tannivṛttiradhārṣṭyam. apragalbhatve kātaratve vartate. klībate, klībāñcakre.

meanings.English: to lack boldness, to be timid, to lose courage, to be impotent or unmanly
meanings.Tamil: dhairiyamatra nilai aṭai, kōḻaiyāka iru, tayakkam aṭai
meanings.Hindi: kāyaratā dikhānā, himmat hārnā, apragalbha honā
meanings.Bengali: sāhas hārāno, kāpuruṣatā dekhāno, bhīru howā
meanings.German: verzagt sein, mutlos sein, sich feige benehmen
meanings.French: manquer d'audace, être timoré, agir sans courage
meanings.Russian: byt' truslivym, proyavlyat' robost', teryat' muzhestvo

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhu' means to shake, agitate, or cause to tremble. Because it has an anubandha 'ñ' (ñit), it takes both active endings (Parasmaipada) and middle endings (Atmanepada). When used in Parasmaipada, the action generally flows outwardly toward an external object being shaken, whereas in Atmanepada, the action reflects back upon the agent or is performed for the subject's own sake.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The wind shakes the branch of the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Atmanepada, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The frightened child trembles with fear.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhuñ kampane. ñidantatvad ubhayapaditvam. sarvadhatuke gune 'dhavati', 'dhavate' iti rupe bhavatah. kampanam calanam preranam ca iti arthah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhuñ kampane. anit, ubhayapadi. dhunoti-ityapi svadau pathyate, kintu bhvadau dhavati dhavate iti guna-av-adeshabhyam sidhyati.

meanings.English: to shake, to agitate, to tremble

canonical_dhatvartha: upatāpe (in the sense of affliction, distress, or torment)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root klīś means to suffer distress or to cause torment. In the simple active present tense (kartari prayoga), it conjugates as klīśati to describe someone undergoing pain or affliction. When used in the causative (ṇijanta) form as kleśayati, the meaning shifts to actively causing torment, harassing, or vexing another person or animal.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (third person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The sick child suffers distress.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (third person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person torments animals.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti records the root klīśū with the marker ū indicating optional iṭ in certain non-sarvadhatuka contexts or derived forms. The primary semantic domain is defined under upatāpa (mental or physical suffering and affliction). The standard present class-1 derivation yields klīśati with standard guna blocked in unaugmented sarvadhatuka contexts.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes klīśū in the sense of upatāpa (torment or bodily/mental suffering). He highlights the phonological stability of the long ī vowel in the primary present stem klīśati and contrasts it with the divadi class kliś-root (kliśyate).

meanings.English: to suffer, to undergo distress, to be afflicted, to torment
meanings.Hindi: kashta pānā, klesha anubhava karnā, duḥkhī honā
meanings.French: souffrir, être affligé, endurer des tourments

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śap' primarily means to curse, swear an oath, or scold someone. In the sense of reviling or taking a solemn oath, Panini prescribes Atmanepada terminations (śapate). When converted into a causative (nic), it takes the meaning 'to make someone take an oath' or 'to cause someone to curse'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (present tense, 3rd person singular, Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The sage curses the wicked person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic-pratyaya, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: causes to swear an oath / administers an oath
scenarios.example_english: The king makes the soldier swear by the truth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'śapa ākrośe' as denoting vituperation, calling down misfortune, or taking a pledge. By the special rule 'śapa upālambhane', Atmanepada endings are systematically employed when expressing censure or an oath.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'śap' belongs to the anit series within the Bhvadi-gana, taking guna strengthening of the radical vowel in non-afflicted positions, forming 'śapate' in the sense of akrosha (imprecation or oath-taking).

meanings.English: to curse, to swear an oath, to revile

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mal' means 'to hold', 'to retain', 'to wear', or 'to bear'. It takes Atmanepada endings because of its anudatta marker in the Paninian recitation. When combined with causative affixes, it conveys making someone hold or wear something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), Prathama-purusha (third person), Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sage holds a wooden staff.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to hold / makes someone wear
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the child wear an ornament.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The dhatu ṭumala is listed under the Bhvadi class in the sense of 'dharana' (holding or sustaining). Because of the anudatta anubandha marker, it operates strictly in the Atmanepada in unaugmented active constructions, yielding forms such as malate, mamale, and malita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mala dharane', defining dharana as poshana (nurturing/supporting) or dharana (holding/bearing). The primary finite present form is malate.

meanings.English: to hold, to bear, to wear, to sustain

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mī' means to harm, hurt, injure, or destroy. Because it has a silent marker 'ṅ' (mīṅ), it takes Atmanepada endings in its normal active voice, changing its core vowel to 'ay' before vowel-initial conjugational suffixes to form 'mayate'. In causative forms, it takes 'ṇic' to mean causing harm or causing destruction.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Atmanepada, Prathama purusha (3rd person), Ekavacana (singular), Lat lakara (present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person harms the virtuous person without any reason.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic), Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana, Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: Causes to harm or destroys through someone else
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the enemy to be harmed by his soldiers.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mīṅ hiṃsāyām' belongs to the Bhvadi class and takes Atmanepada markers due to the anubandha 'ṅ'. In Sarvadhatuka environments with the infix 'śap', the root undergoes guna to 'me' and subsequently 'ay'-ādeśa before vowels, yielding 'mayate'. It is classified as anit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mīṅ hiṃsāyām' as an Atmanepadi root expressing injury, killing, or destruction. The transformation follows standard Bhvadi guna and sandhi rules for an i-ending root, resulting in 'mayate' in the present tense.

meanings.English: to injure, to harm, to hurt, to kill, to destroy
meanings.Hindi: chot pahunchana, himsa karna, vinash karna
meanings.Bengali: aghat kora, himsa kora, dhvongsho kora
meanings.French: blesser, faire du mal, tuer, détruire

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhūp' means to burn, heat, fumigate, or suffer distress/heat. Under Paninian rule 3.1.28 ('gup-dhūp-vicchi-paṇi-panebhyaḥ āyaḥ'), it optionally takes the suffix 'āya' in active usage, producing 'dhūpāyati' alongside the simple form 'dhopati'. When used as a causative (nic), it conveys causing to fumigate or burning incense.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (present indicative active with optional aya-pratyaya, Panini 3.1.28)
scenarios.meaning: Burns incense / fumigates / feels heated or distressed
scenarios.example_english: The devotee burns fragrant incense in the temple.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative active (nic-pratyaya, Kartari prayoga)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to fumigate or purifies with fragrant smoke
scenarios.example_english: The priest fumigates all directions with holy incense.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhūpa santāpe - idam bhvādau paṭhyate. 'gupdhūpvicchipanipanebhya āyaḥ' iti āyapratyaye kṛte 'dhūpāyati' iti rūpam. āyābhāve guṇe 'dhopati' ityapi kecit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhūpa santāpe - santāpaḥ taptībhāvaḥ paritāpo vā. dhūpāyati, dhūpayati. dhūpaḥ iti bhāve ghañ.

meanings.English: to heat, burn incense, fumigate, or feel distressed
meanings.Bengali: dhup deya, tatta haoya, santap kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hlech' means to speak indistinctly, utter indistinct sounds, or mumble. In basic form (Parasmaipada), it describes an individual babbling or speaking unclearly. In causative forms, it denotes causing someone to mutter or produce unclear speech.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The confused child mumbles indistinctly out of fear.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to speak indistinctly or mutters through someone
scenarios.example_english: Intoxication causes the traveler to speak indistinctly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'hlecha' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with the meaning 'avyaktayam vaci' (indistinct or inarticulate speech). Being an inarticulate vocalization root, it behaves morphologically parallel to 'mleccha', forming present stems with parasmaipada personal endings (hlecchati).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'hlecha' alongside 'mleccha' under the meaning of indistinct or barbarous utterance ('avyakta-shabde'). It takes the standard thematic vikarana 'sap' without nasal infixation, taking set endings in non-sarvadhatuka forms.

meanings.English: to speak indistinctly, to utter inarticulate sounds, to mumble

transitivity: Intransitive (or Transitive in the sense of stealing)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gluc' means to go, to creep, or to move stealthily. In simple present active tense (Parasmaipada), it forms 'glucati', describing someone moving quietly or slipping away. In the causative form (Nich), it becomes 'glocayati', which means to cause someone or something to move or sneak away.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple Present (Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Kartari Prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The thief slips away in the dark.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nich-pratyaya, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: causes to move / makes sneak away
scenarios.example_english: The commander makes the soldier advance stealthily along the path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'glucu' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana and ends in the unvoiced palatal stop 'ca'. It is primarily used in the sense of motion (gatau) and stealthy withdrawal (steye/apanaye). It takes the standard Shap vikaranaprattaya in Sarvadhatuka environments to yield the stem gluca-.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin classifies 'glucu' alongside 'prucu', 'mrucu', and 'mlucu' as roots denoting motion, creeping, and clandestine movement. It inflects identically to other simple palatal-ending Bhvadi Parasmaipada roots, forming glucati, gluloca, and glocita/glucitah.

meanings.English: to go, to creep, to slip away, to steal away
meanings.Tamil: selluthal, marainthu selluthal, thiruttu thanamaga povathu
meanings.Hindi: jana, khisakna, chupke se nikal jana

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pru' means to leap, spring, or move swiftly. Because it has an indicative 'ṅ' (anudāttet), it strictly takes Ātmanepada endings in basic active voice (Kartari). When used in the causative (ṇijanta), it typically switches to Parasmaipada endings to express causing someone or something to leap or move.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer leaps swiftly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇijanta (causative), laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The rider makes the horse leap over the ditch.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'pruṅ gatau' as an anudāttet (Ātmanepada) and aniṭ root. By applying the standard guṇa substitution to the root vowel 'u' before the sārvadhātuka affix 'śap', the form 'pravate' is derived (pru + śap + te = pravate). It forms the perfect tense as 'puprāve'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini classifies 'pruṅ' in the sense of motion (gatau), particularly motion involving leaping or springing similar to 'pluṅ'. It confirms the aniṭ nature and lists standard formations such as 'pravate', perfect 'puprāve', and causative 'prāvayati'.

meanings.English: to leap, spring, jump, or move swiftly

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'val' fundamentally means to cover, surround, encircle, or turn/move. In basic everyday usage, it takes Atmanepada endings (valate) to denote turning or covering around something. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it forms 'valayati' or 'valayate', meaning to cause to turn or to surround/enclose something like a bracelet (valaya).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), Prathama-purusha (third person), Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The creeper turns and winds due to the force of the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to move, encircles, or fastens around
scenarios.example_english: The girl winds the sacred thread around her hand.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya clarifies 'vala samvarane' as denoting covering, concealing, or enclosing (accladana/samvarana). Belonging to the jvaladi group, it takes mittva in specific causative operations where short vowel alternatives apply, yielding forms such as valate, vavale, valita, and valanam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'vala samvarane' implies 'avaranarthata' (covering or enveloping) as well as subtle circular movement (gati-vishesha). Forms in primary conjugations are Atmanepadi ('valate'), highlighting internal movement and surrounding action.

meanings.English: To cover, to surround, to enclose, to turn, to move

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'muc' (muñc) in the first conjugation means to be happy, delighted, or to rejoice. Because it has an 'i' marker in the Dhatupatha, it gains a nasal sound 'n' inside the root, forming 'muñcati' in the present tense.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (Present tense, Active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The child rejoices with his friend.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative form)
scenarios.example_english: The father makes his son happy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mucĩ' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read in the sense of 'pramoda' (delight or rejoicing). As it is marked with the indicatory letter 'i' (idit), the augment num is inserted by the rule 'idito num dhātoḥ', giving the base form 'muñc-'. In the present tense, it conjugates as muñcati, muñcataḥ, muñcanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mucĩ pramode', emphasizing the semantic sense of rejoicing and gladdening. He explains the insertion of the nasal letter due to its idit classification and confirms its standard Parasmaipada inflection as 'muñcati'.

meanings.English: to rejoice, to delight, to be happy

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khyā' fundamentally denotes telling, recounting, or declaring. Marked with 'ñ', it is an Ubhayapadi root that predominantly occurs in classical Sanskrit with verbal prefixes (upasargas) like 'ā-' (to narrate/tell) or 'pra-' (to become renowned or celebrated). In active usage, it conveys narrating a story or fact, whereas in passive or reflexive contexts, it expresses gaining fame or being proclaimed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Active Voice) with 'ā' upasarga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother narrates a story to the child.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Karmani/Bhave prayoga (Passive/Reflexive) with 'pra' upasarga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: is renowned / is celebrated / is proclaimed
scenarios.example_english: The scholar is renowned everywhere for virtues.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: khyāñ prakathane: ñid-anubandha-balād ubhayapadatvam. prakathanam vistarataḥ kathanam ucyate. prayogeṣu prāyaśa upasarga-pūrvaka eva dṛśyate yathā ākhyāti prakhyātīti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: khyāñ prakathane: kathana-kriyāyām vartate. ñit-pratyayena parasmaipada-ātmanepadayoḥ pravṛttiḥ.

meanings.English: to tell, narrate, declare, recount, or make known
meanings.Hindi: kahanā, batānā, varnana karanā, prakhyāta honā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kap' means to move, shake, or tremble. By default, it takes Atmanepada endings to express an intransitive shaking motion experienced by the subject. When the causative suffix (Nic) is added, it transitions into a transitive action meaning to cause something to shake or stir.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The tree shakes due to the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The storm causes the mountain peaks to shake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti treats 'kapa cale' as an Atmanepadi root belonging to the Bhvadi class. Being inherently connected with involuntary or natural movement (calana), it forms present indicative singular as 'kapate'. Under causative formation with Nic, it lengthens its penultimate vowel to yield 'kāpayati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'kapa cale' that this root denotes physical trembling, vibration, or unsteady motion. It is classified in the middle set of Bhvadi roots which retain Atmanepada affixation in normal active voice.

meanings.English: to shake, to tremble, to move

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ghur' means to sound frightful, roar menacingly, snort, or appear terrifying. In the basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject making a harsh, frightening sound or growling. In the causative form (Nic), it conveys making someone else roar, snort, or growl frightfully.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The lion roars fiercely in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative active (Prencana / Nic, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to sound frightfully or roar
scenarios.example_english: The hunter causes the hound to growl menacingly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses 'ghura bhime' indicating the production of a frightful, terrible sound or intimidating behavior. It takes the shab-vikarana in sarvadhatuka tenses, undergoes guna of the penultimate short vowel to form 'ghorati', and forms periphrastic and reduplicated perfect stems with set characteristics (jughora, ghorita).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the root 'ghur' in the sense of terrifying roar or fearful manifestation ('bhime bhayamkaranade'). It is grouped alongside roots denoting harsh, forceful sound production and retains Parasmaipada endings with set operation in ardhadhatuka affixes.

meanings.English: to sound frightfully, to roar, to growl, to snort

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhās' means to shine, glitter, or become evident. It belongs to the Bhvādi class and takes Ātmanepada endings. In simple forms it describes things glowing or shining brightly, while in causative forms it describes illuminating or making something evident.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative, 3rd person singular, Ātmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The sun shines in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Ṇijanta), Kartari prayoga, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The lamp illuminates the house.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root bhāsa is listed in the Bhvādi class with the meaning dīptau (to shine, radiate, or illuminate). It is anudāttet, thereby taking exclusively Ātmanepada affixes in primary conjugation, and forms bhāsate, babhāse, bhāsitā, bhāsiṣyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes bhāsa dīptau as an inherently radiant verbal root. The base forms regular guna-less stems since the radical vowel is already dirgha (bhās-a-te) and retains seṭ characteristics in the non-sarvadhatuka affixes.

meanings.English: to shine, to glitter, to appear, to illuminate
meanings.Bengali: ujjvala haoyā, prakāśita haoyā, sobhā pāoyā

it_status: Anit (historically / in standard classical derivation forms: anit in perfect and certain primary affixes, set in future/s-aorist)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'has' fundamentally means 'to laugh' or 'to smile'. Because it is an intransitive verb (akarmaka), it does not take a direct object in normal active usage. When used in simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it shows a person laughing naturally. When combined with prefixes (upasargas) like 'pra-' (loud laughing), 'vi-' (gentle smiling), or 'apa-' (ridiculing), or turned into a causative (hasayati), its expression shifts clearly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Third Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy laughs at his friend's words.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative, Third Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to laugh / makes laugh
scenarios.example_english: The jester makes all people laugh.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'hase~ hasane' as denoting facial cheerfulness, pleasant sound, and laughter (vikasatmika mukhadi-kriya). It operates as an intransitive (akarmaka) root in Kartari Parasmaipada, forming 'hasati', perfect 'jahasa', and causative 'hasayati'. Prefixations like 'prahasati' signify loud laughter, whereas 'apahasati' conveys mocking or derision.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini specifies 'hasa hasane' as an active root with dental sibilant 'sa'. It forms regular secondary derivatives like 'hasita' (smiled/laughed) and 'hasyam' (laughter/humor). The root maintains regular guna in sarvadhatuka environments and reduplication as 'jahasa' in lit-lakkara.

meanings.English: to laugh, smile, ridicule
meanings.Bengali: hasha, mukhe hasi photano, thak-upahas kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svad' means to taste, savor, relish, or to be pleasing and sweet. In its standard primary voice (Atmanepada), it denotes someone tasting or experiencing the deliciousness of food. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it shifts to 'svadayati' meaning to make something palatable, sweeten, or season food.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha (3rd person singular), Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The boy relishes the sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the pudding sweet with sugar.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'svada asvadane' as an Atmanepadi, set root in the Bhvadi-gana. It notes that the root denotes the perception of taste (rasanendriya-vyapara) as well as finding pleasure or sweetness (modana/tripti). Morphological forms derived include the present 'svadate', perfect 'sasvade', and aorist 'asvadishta'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'svada' under the sense of relish and pleasantness ('svad asvadane modane ca'). He emphasizes that while the primary root functions in the Atmanepada ('svadate phalam'), in secondary or causative usage ('svadayati / svadayate') it signifies rendering an object tasteful or savory.

meanings.English: to taste, relish, savor, be pleasing

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhṛ' means to hold, carry, support, or nourish. Because it has an 'ñ' marker (ñit), it can be conjugated in both Parasmaipada (active) and Atmanepada (middle). In Parasmaipada, it often expresses carrying or supporting something externally. In Atmanepada, it highlights holding or nourishing for oneself. When used with a causative suffix (ṇic), it changes to 'bhārayati', meaning 'causes to carry or support'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (Parasmaipada, 3rd person singular, lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The man carries the load on his head.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (Atmanepada, 3rd person singular, lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The father supports his own family.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇijanta (causative, Parasmaipada, lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The master makes the servant carry the load.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: bhṛñ dhāraṇapoṣaṇayoḥ. ñitvād ubhayapadī. anupadeśe aniṭ. guṇe raparatve ca bharatīti bhavati. dhāraṇaṃ dehadhāraṇam, poṣaṇaṃ vardhanam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: bhṛñ dhāraṇe poṣaṇe ca. bhṛñ ityubhayatobhāṣā. guṇādeśe 'bharati' 'bharate' ityādi rūpam. dharati poṣayati ceti arthaḥ.

meanings.English: to bear, carry, support, or nourish
meanings.Bengali: dharana kara, poshana kara, baha kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mluc' means to go, move, or bend/set. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), the vowel 'u' takes Guna strengthening to become 'o', producing the present form 'mlocati' (he/she goes or sets). In causative constructions with the affix Nic, it means 'causes to go' or 'causes to set', appearing as 'mlocayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense / Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The sun moves (sets) towards the mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to move / causes to descend
scenarios.example_english: Time causes everything to move along.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti specifies 'mluca gatau' as an intransitive root signifying general movement or descending motion. Due to being Anit, it takes no intermediate i-agama in standard unaugmented non-sarvadhatuka forms like mloksyati and amlocat.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'mluc' belongs to the series of motion roots (mluc, mroc, gruc, groc) sharing the meaning 'gatau'. The radical vowel 'u' undergoes regular Guna to 'o' in Sarvadhatuka contexts giving 'mlocati'.

meanings.English: to go, move, wander, or set/descend
meanings.Hindi: jana, chalna, doobna ya asta hona

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gup' fundamentally denotes hiding, guarding, or concealing. In everyday usage, it takes special affixes: with the suffix 'aya' (svarthe aya) it conjugates in Parasmaipada as 'gopayati' meaning 'to protect or guard', whereas with the desiderative affix 'san' it takes Atmanepada as 'jugupsate' meaning 'to despise, avoid, or shrink away from'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: aya-pratyaya in svarthe (protection sense)
scenarios.example_english: The king protects the citizens through righteousness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: san-pratyaya with ninda/heya sense (Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The virtuous person shrinks away from sinful acts.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti highlights that the root 'gup' takes the optional or mandatory 'aya' suffix by Panini's sutra 'gupudhupavicipanipanibhya ayah' in the sense of preservation and protection (gopayati), and mandatory 'san' by 'gup-tij-kidbhyah san' yielding 'jugupsate' in the sense of aversion and moral distancing (ninda/jugupsa).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini emphasizes the dual semantic domains of 'gup': secret protection/concealment (rakshane gopane ca) seen in forms like 'gopayati' and censure/avoidance (dosadarshana) seen in 'jugupsate'.

meanings.English: to protect, conceal, or shrink away from

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'math' means to churn, agitate, or stir vigorously. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent actively churning or stirring something like milk or ocean waters. In the causative form (Nic), it means causing someone to churn or intensely agitating a substance or mind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present Tense (Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd girl churns the curd.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic Pratyaya), Present Tense (Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: Anger agitates the mind.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'matha vilolane' belongs to the Bhvadi class. 'Vilolana' denotes physical shaking, stirring, or churning. Being an adanta/idanta context or simple akaranta base, it forms 'mathati' with the shap-pratyaya in sarvadhatuka contexts.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'matha vilolane' as an action of thorough stirring and disturbance of a liquid or matter, yielding forms like mathati, mamatha, mathita.

meanings.English: To churn, to stir, to agitate

pada: Atmanepada (Parasmaipada with upasargas vi, a, pari)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ram' fundamentally means to rejoice, play, or take delight. In its standard form, it takes Atmanepada endings (ramate - one delights). However, under Paninian rule 1.3.83 (vyaparibhyo ramah), when prefixed with upasargas like 'vi-', 'a-', or 'pari-', the verb switches to Parasmaipada and shifts meaning to desisting, stopping, or pausing (viramati - stops/abstains). In the causative form, it means to entertain or please someone (ramayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present indicative, standard Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The child rejoices in the garden.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga with upasarga 'vi' (governed by sutra vyaparibhyo ramah)
scenarios.example_english: The noble person abstains from sin.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ramu' is marked with anudatta it and categorized under anit roots. Its canonical sense is 'krida' (play, revelry, sporting). By default, it takes Atmanepada affixes. Madhava highlights special syntactic conditions, such as the mandatory shift to Parasmaipada when preceded by the preverbs 'vi', 'a', and 'pari', as well as morpho-phonemic operations in kit/nit suffixes and lit reduplication forms like 'reme'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'krida' as vihara (recreation) or prenkharadi. He notes the vocalic modifications under various lakaras, detailing the elision and retention of the final nasal consonant in non-sarvadhatuka contexts, as well as the transition from akarmaka (intransitive enjoyment) to sakarmaka/virodhartha contexts depending on upasarga collocations.

meanings.English: to delight, to rejoice, to play, to take pleasure in
meanings.Hindi: anand lena, ramna, prasanna hona, khelna
meanings.Bengali: ananda pawa, raman kara, khela kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svid' primarily means to become moist, to sweat, or to experience oily perspiration/affection. Because it is marked with an anudatta vowel marker in the Dhatupatha, it operates natively in Atmanepada (svedate) to denote personal sweating or moisturizing. When the causative suffix (Nic) is added, it switches to Parasmaipada/Ubhayapada (svedayati) meaning to cause someone to perspire, steam, or foment medically.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_sanskrit: tapasi krite shramena shramiko bhrisham svedate.
scenarios.example_english: Due to physical labor in the heat, the worker perspires profusely.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The physician foments the patient with medicinal steam.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya clarifies ñisvida snehane as belonging to the dyutadi subgroup of Bhvadi. The initial 'ñi' is an it-marker signifying the applicability of specific secondary affixes, and the final anudatta vowel dictates Atmanepada. It denotes moistening, unctuousness, or sweating (svedana).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes the root as 'svida snehane', glossed with the sense of svedana (perspiring) and snigdhikarana (making greasy or soft). Belonging to the dyutadi class, it takes guna in sarvadhatuka affixes yielding 'svedate'.

meanings.English: to sweat, perspire, become moist or unctuous
meanings.Hindi: pasina chhutna, svedana hona, chikna hona

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'krak' means to thicken, congeal, or gather densely into a mass. In its basic Parasmaipada form, it describes the subject itself becoming thick, coagulated, or dense. When used with causative markers (Nic), it changes the meaning to actively causing something to congeal or mass together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active indicative, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The milk thickens due to heat.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative Active, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.meaning: causes to congeal or thickens something
scenarios.example_english: The cook thickens the sweet pudding.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'krak' is read in the Bhvadi Gana with the semantic marker 'samstyane', which denotes density, coagulation, or compaction (sanghata/ghanibhava). Being anidit and haladi, it forms 'krakati' in the present indicative without nasalization.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'krak samstyane' signifying becoming compact or consolidated (ghanibhave). It follows the standard Bhvadi inflectional paradigm with standard Set behavior in appropriate ardhadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to congeal, coagulate, thicken, become dense

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'churc' means to hurt, injure, or cause pain to someone. In the standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it shows someone causing injury directly. When converted into the causative form using 'nic' affix (chorcayati), it means causing someone else to hurt or injure an individual.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense active voice, 3rd person singular, lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person injures the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative form, lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the enemy to be hurt.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: churca himsayam. dantya-talavyadir dvitiyavan. churcati, acurchit. iditvat na num, it-samjna-lopadi karyam. upadhayam guna-abhave sati churcati iti rupam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: churca himsayam. churcati. churcitas-tavya-ityadavapi setvat idagamah bhavati.

meanings.English: to injure, to hurt, to do violence

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mruñc' primarily conveys moving in a crooked, winding, or stealthy manner, or entering into an obscure/impenetrable place. In active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent moving stealthily or vanishing. When modified with the causative suffix (Nic), it shifts to mean causing someone or something to move stealthily or leading someone through a hidden route.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: He/she moves stealthily or walks crookedly
scenarios.example_english: The thief moves stealthily in the dense forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: Causes to slip away or guides stealthily
scenarios.example_english: The commander makes the soldier move covertly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mruñcā gatigahanayoḥ. gatikautilye gahane duravagahe praveshe cha vartate. mroñcati, mumroñca, mroñcita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mruñcā gatau gahanatve cha. kautilyena gamanam gahanam va mroñcanam. mroñcati.

meanings.English: to move crookedly, to go stealthily, to slip away
meanings.French: se faufiler, aller de travers, se glisser
meanings.Chinese: wan yan qian xing, qian xing

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣap' belongs to the 1st class (Bhvadi) and is conjugated in the Atmanepada. It expresses the core action of urging, impelling, sending forth, or casting. When used in normal kartari (active) voice, it indicates urging oneself or discharging an action with internal involvement. In the causative (nic) form, it signifies making someone else impel or dispatch something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (Bhvadi Atmanepada)
scenarios.meaning: He/she impels, urges, or sends forth.
scenarios.example_english: The rider urges the horse for speed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/she causes to urge or dispatches.
scenarios.example_english: The master makes the messenger hurry forth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kṣapa prerane | anudattettvad atmanepadi | kshapate | cakshape | kshapita | kshapishyate | preranamutsahah prerana va |
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kṣapa prerane | preranam prekshepo viddhirva | kshapate, cakshape, kshapishyati na bhavati anudattettvat |

meanings.English: to impel, to urge, to dispatch, to throw

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vres' describes living in distress, poverty, or surviving with great difficulty. In basic active forms (Parasmaipada), it shows someone struggling to make a living. In causative forms, it means forcing or causing someone to live under severe hardship.
