dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root push means to nourish, cherish, foster, or to grow strong and thrive. In the 4th class (Divadi gana), it adds the middle sound -ya- (shyan) to form pushyati in active voice (Parasmaipada). When we want to say someone is making another person foster or nurture, we add the causative marker -aya- (nic) to get poshayati.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Divadi gana active present indicative (lat, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana with shyan vikarana)
scenarios.example_english: The mother nourishes her son with affection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative present active (nijanta lat, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana)
scenarios.example_english: The father fosters the trees with water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies pusha pushtau in the Divadi-gana as an anit, parasmaipadi root taking the shyan affix to yield pushyati. It distinguishes this fourth-class presentation from identical roots in other ganas (such as Kryadi pushnati), emphasizing the intrinsic semantic value of bodily and spiritual flourishing (pushti).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes pusha pushtau as denoting growth, support, and plenitude. The text details the phonological behavior under anit conditions and describes its usage in both transitive senses (supporting another) and intransitive development (attaining bodily vigor).

meanings.English: to nourish, to foster, to cherish, to thrive
meanings.Bengali: poshana kara, palana kara, pushta haoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tras' belongs to the Divadi gana (Class 4) and conveys the sense of feeling fear, being alarmed, or trembling from agitation. By default, it takes the class marker 'ya' (Syan) yielding 'trasyati'. By Panini's rule 'va bhrasabhlasabhramuklamutrasitrutilasah', it can also optionally take the Bhvadi marker 'a' (Sap), producing 'trasati'. When made causative with 'nic', it becomes 'trasayati' (frightens/scares someone).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Divadi Parasmaipada Lat Lakara (Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana) with Syan vikaranapratyaya
scenarios.example_english: The deer is terrified of the lion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic) Parasmaipada Lat Lakara (Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The roaring thunder frightens the young boy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: trasī udvege. udvego bhayam calanam va. trasyati. 'va bhrasabhlasabhramuklamutrasitrutilasah' iti pakshe sap - trasati. anudattetvabhava upadhadirgho na bhavati. nic-pratyaye trasayati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: trasī udvege. udvega ih kampanam bhayam ca. trasyati, trasati. udvijate trasyatiti paryayah.

meanings.English: to tremble, to fear, to be terrified or agitated

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'so' means to finish, terminate, or bring to an end. Belonging to the 4th conjugation (Divadi gana), it takes the Vikarana affix 'shyan' (-ya-) in the present system, turning 'so' into 'sya-', conjugated in Parasmaipada as 'syati'. When combined with prefixes (upasargas) such as 'ava' or 'vi-ava', it specifically denotes concluding, deciding, or striving decisively.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: terminates / finishes / brings to an end
scenarios.example_english: Time brings an end to all sorrow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga with upasarga 'ava', lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The wise person concludes the work quickly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'so' is taught in the sense of 'antakarma' (destruction, conclusion, finishing). It is anit and parasmaipadi. In the presence of the shyan-pratyaya, the root vowel 'o' undergoes the operational changes under 'o dakaropadhayah' and 'aca upadhadharmat', forming 'syati', 'syatah', 'syanti'. The past participle is formed as 'sita' via the 'it' substitution rule for o-karanta roots.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses 'so antakarmani' as vinashe samaptau ca (in the sense of destruction or completion). The forms are syati in lat, sasau in lit, and asat in lun. When prefixed with 'ava', it denotes final determination or cessation (avasanam).

meanings.English: to finish, destroy, bring to an end, conclude
meanings.Hindi: samapta karna, anta karna, vinasha karna
meanings.Bengali: shesh kora, binash kora, samapta kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klam' means to become tired, weary, or exhausted. Because it belongs to the 4th conjugation (Divadi gana) and is part of the special 'samadi' group, the short 'a' becomes long 'a' before the present tense marker 'ya' (syan), giving forms like 'klamyati' (he/she gets tired). In the causative form, it takes the nic suffix, meaning 'to cause someone to become exhausted'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The traveler gets fatigued due to the long journey.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The intense heat exhausts the farmer.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'klamu' is defined in the sense of 'glani' (physical or mental exhaustion/languor). Being part of the 'samadi' subclass of Divadit, the vowel lengthens by the rule 'samamastanam dirghah syani' in sarvadhatuka contexts before 'syan', yielding 'klamyati'. In nishtha (kta/ktavatu), the regular form is 'klanta' with elision of 'm' and compensatory lengthening.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'klamu glanau' as an intransitive root denoting the state of fatigue or loss of vigor. It patterns with 'sam', 'dam', and 'bhram' in undergoing dirgha-adesha under syan affixation ('klamyati'), and forms 'klantah' as an adjective/participle denoting tired or faded.

meanings.English: to be fatigued, to become exhausted, to weary, to fade
meanings.Bengali: klanta haoya, abasanna haoya, mlan haoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ruṣ' means to become angry or enraged. As a Class 4 (Divadi) root, it adds '-ya-' (śyan) to form its base, resulting in 'ruṣyati' in the active voice. When used with a causative suffix (ṇic), it changes to 'roṣayati', shifting the meaning from 'becoming angry' to 'making someone else angry' or 'provoking'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative, 3rd person singular with śyan vikarana)
scenarios.example_english: Even at gentle words, the foolish person becomes angry.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic prayoga (Causative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: He enrages his friend with untrue words.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ruṣa roṣe - divādiraniṭ parasmaipadī. roṣaḥ kopaḥ. śyani prāpte 'ruṣyati' iti rūpam. liṭi ruroṣa, luṅi tu aroṣīt arukṣat vā. ṇici roṣayati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ruṣa roṣe - roṣe vartamānaḥ puṣyādiraniṭ. ruṣyati, ruroṣa, roṣṭā, roṣyati. krodhārtho 'yam akarmakaḥ sakarmakaśca prasiddhaḥ.

meanings.English: to be angry, to get enraged, to be annoyed
meanings.Hindi: krodhit hona, gussa hona, rusht hona
meanings.Bengali: kruddha haoya, rag kora, rushta haoya
meanings.German: zornig sein, sich argern, wutend werden
meanings.French: se facher, etre en colere, s'irriter

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣap' belongs to the 4th class (Divadi gana) and primarily means to destroy, diminish, or harm. In the present tense, it takes the class marker 'ya' (Śyan) to form 'kṣapyati'. When used in the causative form with 'ṇic', it becomes 'kṣapayati', which commonly denotes causing destruction, wasting, or spending/passing time.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice, present tense, 3rd person singular with Śyan vikarana)
scenarios.example_english: Disease destroys (weakens) the body.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇyanta (causative active voice, present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: A fool wastes time in vain.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kṣapā himsayām kṣaye ca. divādiṣu paṭhitaḥ parasmaipadī aniṭ. śyanapratyaye kṣapyati. ṇici kṣapayati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kṣapā himse kṣaye vā. kṣapyati, cakṣāpa, kṣapsyati. śyani guṇābhāvaḥ.

meanings.English: to destroy, to harm, to diminish, to waste
meanings.Hindi: nasht karna, kshin karna, vinash karna
meanings.Bengali: dhangsho kora, khoy kora, binash kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klam' means to become fatigued, tired, or to wither. Belonging to the Divadi group (4th class), it takes the marker 'syan' to form 'klamyati' (lengthened to klamyati by rule 'shama-tam-ashtanam dirghah shyani'). When a causative suffix (Nic) is added, it changes from 'feeling tired' to 'exhausting or tiring someone else' ('klamayati').

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Divadi gana (syan pratyaya with stem lengthening)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler feels fatigued due to the long path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya)
scenarios.meaning: causes to become exhausted / wears out
scenarios.example_english: The intense heat exhausts the farmer.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'klamu glanau' belongs to the shamadi group of the Divadi gana. In sarvadhatuka affixes with syan, the radical vowel undergoes dirgha (lengthening) by the sutra 'shamashtanam dirghah shyani' (7.3.74), yielding 'klamyati'. In the past passive participle, the nipatana form 'klanta' is obtained without the intermediate it-augment.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'klamu glanau' within the Divadi class. It expresses exhaustion, mental depression, or physical withering. He highlights its membership in the eight roots beginning with 'shama' that receive penult vowel lengthening before syan.

meanings.English: to be fatigued, to feel exhausted, to wither

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'puṣ' belongs to the 4th conjugation (Divādi class) and takes the 'śyan' affix (-ya-) in standard active voice (Parasmaipada) to mean 'to nourish', 'to thrive', or 'to foster'. In the simple active present tense, it forms 'puṣyati' (he/she thrives or nourishes). When made causative (ṇic), it forms 'poṣayati', meaning 'causes to nourish or sustain' someone else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Divādi class active voice (kartari prayoga) with śyan pratyaya
scenarios.example_english: The tree thrives with water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative affix (ṇic pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The mother nourishes the child with milk.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'puṣa puṣṭau' under the Divādi group as an aniṭ root that takes the śyan vikarana in kartari. In the basic present tense, guṇa does not take place before the sārvadhātuka śyan suffix due to its ṅit status, producing the form 'puṣyati'. In secondary formations and liṭ, it exhibits regular guṇa (pupoṣa).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'puṣa' denotes bodily growth, nourishment, and fullness (puṣṭi). As an aniṭ root of the Divādi class, it operates both intransitively (to flourish/grow) and transitively (to foster/feed), distinguishing it from homophonous forms in the Kryādi or Bhvādi groups.

meanings.English: to nourish, to thrive, to flourish, to foster
meanings.Bengali: poshana kara, pushta haoya, palana kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root tras means to tremble, fear, or become agitated with fright. In basic active voice (Kartari Prayoga) of the 4th class (Divadi), it takes the affix 'syan' to form trasyati. When used as a causative (Nich), it becomes trasayati or trasayati/trasayati (meaning 'to frighten or terrify someone').

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer is terrified of the lion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich Pratyaya (Causative), Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The lion frightens the deer.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root trasī belongs to Divadi-gana and is marked with an ikara-it (indicating optional nasal insertion or specific grammatical operations in classical views). It signifies udvega (fear, agitation, or distress). In the Sarvadhatuka tenses, it takes the class sign syan to yield trasyati, though by special rule 'va bhrasa-bhramu-klamu-trasi-trasa-trut-lasam' it can optionally form trasati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'trasi udvege' signifies fright or quivering due to fear (bhayacalane). It belongs to the Divadi group having Parasmaipada inflections and operates with optional forms across certain conjugational categories.

meanings.English: to tremble, to fear, to be terrified, to be agitated

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ksham' means to forgive, endure, or tolerate. In the 4th class (Divadi), it typically takes the suffix 'syan' to form 'kshamyati' in the active sense (Parasmaipada), expressing the conscious act of bearing a hardship or forgiving a mistake. When used in the causative form (kshamayati), it means causing someone to forgive or seeking pardon.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (Present tense), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana with Divadi affix 'syan'
scenarios.example_english: The noble person forgives the offense.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara
scenarios.meaning: He/She asks for forgiveness or appeases
scenarios.example_english: The disciple asks the teacher for forgiveness.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kshamu sahane' belongs to Divadi gana and is primarily Parasmaipada. By the sutra 'kshamo 'nyatarasyam' (3.1.90), it optionally takes the vikarana 'shap' alongside 'syan', allowing forms like kshamyati, kshamati, and kshamate in various traditional usages. It is characterized as anit in general reduplicated and non-causative environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kshamu sahane' as bearing, patient endurance, or pardoning. He highlights that in the Divadi class, the root exhibits alternate conjugation patterns between the 4th and 1st classes, meaning tolerance of pain, insult, or burden.

meanings.English: to forgive, to endure, to tolerate, to be patient

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'as' belongs to the 4th class (Divadi gana) and primarily means 'to throw', 'to cast', or 'to shoot'. It takes the infix 'ya' (syan) before endings in active voice, becoming 'asyati'. Prefixing preverbs (upasargas) changes the direction or concept of throwing; for example, adding 'abhi' creates 'abhyasyati', which metaphorically means 'to throw oneself repeatedly into learning' or 'to practice'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior shoots an arrow towards the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga with upasarga 'abhi'
scenarios.example_english: The student practices reading in the morning.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti defines 'asu ksepane' as an anudattet, parasmaipadi root of the Divadi class. Due to the syan vikarana, it forms 'asyati'. In perfect tense (lit), reduplication yields 'asa', and future forms include 'asisyati'. Sayana highlights its distinction from the Adadi root 'as' (sattayam) which denotes existence.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'asu' functions in the sense of projection, discharge, or ejection (ksepana). From this root, with the instrumental suffix 'stran', the noun 'astra' (a projectile or missile weapon) is regularly derived, confirming the fundamental sense of propelling outward.

meanings.English: to throw, cast, shoot, hurl, discharge

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kup expresses the emotion of anger or becoming enraged. In standard present tense (kartari prayoga), it belongs to the 4th class (Divadi) and takes the vikaranapratyaya 'syan' (-ya-) without undergoing vowel strengthening (guna), yielding 'kupyati'. When someone causes another to become angry, the causative suffix (nic) is added to form 'kopayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (with syan pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The teacher does not get angry at the student.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person makes everyone angry by his behavior.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya explains 'kupa kope' as denoting mental agitation or anger. Belonging to Divadi, it receives the 'syan' vikaranapratyaya in sarvadhatuka affixes. Since 'syan' is considered nit (having an indicatory n), the penultimate vowel 'u' is blocked from guna, yielding 'kupyati'. In ardhadhatuka forms, guna occurs as in 'cukopa' and 'kopita'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'kupa kope' among the roots signifying internal emotional states (krodhartha). He highlights the unstrengthened radical vowel under the influence of the Divadi marker 'syan' and notes its standard intransitive nature where the target of anger takes the dative case (sampradana) by Paninian rule 'krudhadruhershyasuyarthanam yam prati kopah'.

meanings.English: to be angry, to become enraged, to boil with wrath
meanings.Hindi: krodhit hona, gussa hona, kop karna
meanings.Bengali: kruddho haoya, raag kora, krodh prakash kora
meanings.French: se facher, se mettre en colere, s'irriter
meanings.Chinese: fa nu, sheng qi, fen nu

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bus' belongs to the 4th conjugation (divadi gana), which takes the 'syan' (ya) infix in present stem formations. It conveys the action of releasing, emitting, or casting out. In normal active usage (Parasmaipada), the subject performs the act of discharging or expelling something. When converted to a causative form (nic), it means causing someone or something to release or shed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (parasmaipada with syan vikaranapratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The tree sheds a dry leaf.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'busu utsarjane' under the Divadi class. Since it ends with an u-karit indicator, it drops the anubandha to leave 'bus'. Taking the syan affix, it forms 'busyati'. It is anit in standard non-causative ardhadhatuka operations and functions primarily in the sense of releasing, separating, or casting forth.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'busa utsarjane' among the s-ending roots of the fourth gana alongside dasu, kusu, and shusu. The meaning 'utsarjana' signifies abandonment, discharge, or letting go (tyaga / visrijana), conjugated as 'busyati', 'bosa', 'boshyati'.

meanings.English: to release, discharge, emit, or cast off
meanings.Bengali: utsarga kara, tyag kara, chhere deoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dī' belongs to the Divadi class (4th conjugation) and means 'to fly' or 'to soar through the air'. It is used exclusively in Atmanepada. When the 4th class sign 'śyan' is added, the base remains 'dīyate' in the present tense. In causative (Nich), it denotes causing to fly or launching into flight.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (present indicative 3rd person singular with Atmanepada marker)
scenarios.example_english: The bird flies freely in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) in Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: causes to fly / releases into flight
scenarios.example_english: The boy releases the bird into the sky to fly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dīṅ vihāyasā gatau. vihāyasaḥ ākāśaḥ, tatra gamanamityarthaḥ. aniditvāt anṭkaḥ, divāditvāt śyan. dīyate. ḍīṅ-vihāyasā-gatau ityasyaivāyam anurūpaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dīṅ vihāyasā gatau. ākāśayāne vartate. dīyate pakṣī vihāyasi. liṭi didye.

meanings.English: to fly, to soar, to glide in the sky

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'trs' means to become thirsty or to long for something. In the 4th class (Divadi), it adds 'ya' before the endings in basic present tense, giving 'trsyati' (he/she is thirsty). When made causative with 'nic', it means 'to make someone thirsty' or 'to cause longing', taking forms like 'tarsayati'.

scenarios.example_english: The traveler feels thirsty in the desert.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The scorching heat makes the traveler thirsty.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: trsa pipasayam. divaditvat syan. trsyati. trsitah. pipasa iccha-viseshas trsna ca.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: trsa pipasayam. syan. trsyati. trsitah, tarsita. ardhadhatuke guna-vikalpa-vidhih.

meanings.English: to be thirsty, to thirst for, to desire

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mas' belongs to the 4th group (Divadi-gana) and means 'to measure', 'to weigh', or 'to determine the quantity'. In the standard active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes the fourth-class conjugation marker 'syan' (ya) to become 'masyati'. In causative constructions (producing 'masayati'), the meaning changes to 'causes to measure' or 'has something weighed'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active voice, Divadi-gana with 'syan' pratyaya, Present Tense 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The merchant measures the grain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich-pratyaya (Causative formation, Present Tense 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The owner has the goods measured by the attendant.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'masu' is categorized under Divadi-gana in the sense of 'parimana' (measuring, quantifying). Having an indicatory 'u', it takes 'syan' in Sarvadhatuka affixes yielding forms like 'masyati', 'mamasa', and 'masita'/'masta' according to context.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'masu parimane' as an anit root belonging to the Divadi group. It signifies the estimation or measurement of volume and weight.

meanings.English: to measure, to weigh, to determine quantity

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śuṣ' means to dry up, wither, or lose moisture. In the active voice (Divadi class, taking 'ya' vikaraṇa), it describes a subject naturally drying out or withering away. When the causative suffix (ṇic) is applied, it shifts to an active transitive sense meaning 'to dry something up' or 'to parch'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Divadi class with 'śyan' pratyaya
scenarios.example_english: The leaf of the tree withers in the heat of the sun.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) form, Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: causes to dry up / dries something
scenarios.example_english: The sun dries up the lake with its rays.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'śuṣa' belongs to the Divadi group and is classified under the meaning 'śoṣaṇa' (loss of moisture or drying up). It is anit and Parasmaipadi, deriving forms such as 'śuṣyati' in the present tense, and 'śuṣkaḥ' with the kta suffix by the special rule 'śuṣaḥ kaḥ'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'śuṣa śoṣaṇe' as an intransitive root denoting emaciation or dehydration. In the perfect tense it forms 'śuśoṣa', and in the causative it forms 'śoṣayati'.

meanings.English: to dry up, to wither, to desiccate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'druh' means to harbor ill-will, bear malice, or seek to harm someone. In the fourth class (Divadi gana), it takes the marker 'syan' (-ya-) to form 'druhyati'. In Paninian grammar, the person or target against whom malice or anger is directed takes the fourth case (Sampradana / Dative) according to the rule 'krudhadruhershyasuyarthanam yam prati kopah'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present active indicative, 3rd person singular with syan vikarana)
scenarios.meaning: bears malice towards or seeks to harm
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person bears malice towards the righteous person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative, present active indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to commit treason or harm
scenarios.example_english: The enemy causes the brother to harbor treason against the king.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'druha jighamsayam' in the Divadi class. It notes that the root ends in a 'ha' which optionally undergoes replacement with 'gha' or 'dha' before certain consonant affixes (jhali pare), and is anit in non-causative primary conjugations. The meaning encompasses both an internal intent to kill or harm (jighamsa) and open enmity (apakara).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in the Kshiratarangini explains 'druh' under Divadi with the sense of seeking injury or harbor of malice. He highlights the syntactical governance where the object of malice receives the dative case (caturthi vibhakti) by the special sutra 'krudhadruha-...' unless combined with prefixes like 'pra' where accusative may apply under specific conditions.

meanings.English: to bear malice, to seek to hurt or kill, to betray or commit treason

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root dīp belongs to the fourth group (Divadi) and means 'to shine' or 'to glow'. Because it takes the -ya- infix and Atmanepada endings in its basic form, it expresses the subject glowing on its own (e.g., a lamp shining). When converted into the causative form (dīpayati/dīpayate), it changes to mean 'kindling' or 'illuminating' something else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Divadi class present tense Atmanepada (kartari prayoga with yak/śyan pratyaya)

vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dīpī dīptau. īkāro nirdiṣṭaḥ. dīpyate, didepe, dīptā. prakāśane vartate.

meanings.English: to shine, to glow, to be radiant

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhram' means to wander, roam, spin, or be unsteady. In the 4th class (Divadi), it undergoes vowel lengthening (dirgha) by the special rule 'shama-dama-shrama-bhrama...', forming 'bhramyati' (often also occurring as 'bhramati' under Bhvadi gana variation). When used with a causative affix (Nich), it means to cause to spin or make someone wander ('bhramayati').

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Divadi gana (syan pratyaya with dirgha to root vowel)
scenarios.example_english: The deer wanders in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nich pratyaya), Kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The boy spins the wheel.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'bhramu anavasthane' belongs to the shamadi group of Divadi roots. By the rule 'shamadama-shrama-bhrama-kshama-klama-madam dirghah' (7.3.74), the penultimate vowel 'a' is lengthened to 'a' before the shyan affix, yielding 'bhramyati'. It indicates lack of stability, roaming, or revolving.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'bhramu anavasthane calane ca' - it signifies movement without fixed position, spinning, or confusion. In non-shyan contexts or alternate gana attribution (Bhvadi), it forms 'bhramati', while its past participle is 'bhrantah'.

meanings.English: to wander, roam, rotate, be unsteady, be confused
meanings.Chinese: you dang, xuan zhuan, mi huo

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śuṣ' belongs to the 4th group (Divadigaṇa) and takes the affix 'śyan' (-ya-) in standard active forms, meaning 'to dry up' or 'to wither' by itself. When converted into the causative form (nic), it takes the meaning of actively drying something out or making something dry.

vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: śuṣa śoṣaṇe. śuṣyati. śuṣkaḥ 'śuṣaḥ kaḥ' iti ka-pratyayāntatvam.

meanings.English: to dry up, to wither, to become dry

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root klam means to become tired, fatigued, or exhausted. In the basic present tense (Kartari Prayoga), it takes the Class 4 marker (syan) and lengthens its vowel to form klamyati (grows weary). When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it changes meaning from 'feeling tired oneself' to 'making someone else tired' (klamayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (with syan vikarana and shamadi-dirgha)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler grows weary due to the long journey.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The intense heat exhausts the farmer.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root klamu is defined in the sense of glani (exhaustion or languor). Belonging to the Shamadi sub-group within the Divadi class, it undergoes lengthening of the radical vowel before the syan vikarana by the sutra 'shamashtanam dirghah shyani' (7.3.74), yielding klamyati. In the past passive participle with kta, it becomes klanta without it-agama.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines klamu as physical dejection and fatigue. He highlights the application of penultimate vowel lengthening in the sarvadhatuka shyani environment, deriving klamyati, and identifies its anit character in standard participial formations.

meanings.English: to be weary, to be fatigued, to languish
meanings.Bengali: klanta howa, kranta howa, abashanna howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pi' belongs to the fourth conjugation (Divadi gana) and means 'to drink' or 'to absorb'. Because it has an indicator marker 'n' (n-it), it is conjugated exclusively in the Atmanepada voice in basic tenses using the middle affix 'syan' (-ya-), producing the form 'piyate'. In causative constructions (nic), it takes the base 'payayati' or 'payayate' meaning 'to cause someone to drink' or 'to nourish/nurse'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Divadi gana vikaranasyan (-ya-), Atmanepada prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The calf drinks the milk.

scenarios.meaning: causes to drink / feeds liquid to

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'pin pane' in the Divadi class. Due to the 'n' anubandha, it is purely Atmanepadi. With the 'syan' vikarana in kartari, it takes the form 'piyate'. It notes the semelfactive nature of consumption or swelling/absorbing through drinking.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini analyzes 'pin pane' as an Anit root of the Divadi fourth class taking the syan suffix, yielding 'piyate' in the present tense and 'pipye' in the perfect (lit lakara).

meanings.English: to drink, to imbibe, to absorb

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣam' belongs to the 4th class (Divadi gana) and means to endure, tolerate, or forgive. In the present tense, it takes the class sign 'śyan' (-ya-) and undergoes vowel lengthening to form 'kṣāmyati'. In causative (ṇic), it forms 'kṣamayati' meaning to cause someone to forgive or to ask for forgiveness/patience.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Divadishu ksamu sahane. Syanpratyaye krite 'samo darsane' ityadeshadirghatve kshamyatiti rupam bhavati. Sahanartho aparadhasamarpanadishu dharanam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshamu sahane. Kshamyati. Dirgho bhavati syani. Titikshayam anurupa-prayoga-siddhih.

meanings.English: to tolerate, to forgive, to endure, to pardon

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhvas' belongs to the 4th conjugation (Divadi gana) and expresses falling down, perishing, collapsing, or decaying. In standard active usage within this class, it takes the class marker 'śyan' and Atmanepada endings to mean 'perishes' or 'crumbles'. When used with a causative affix (nic), it becomes Parasmaipada/Ubhayapada meaning 'causes to fall' or 'destroys'.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'yas' belongs to the 4th conjugation (Divadi gana) and means to exert oneself, strive, or make an effort. When prefixes (upasargas) are added, its meaning shifts expressively: 'pra-' emphasizes energetic effort or striving, while 'a-' denotes exhaustion or becoming fatigued from heavy exertion.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'yasu' is placed in the Divadi class taking Parasmaipada endings and is anit. It is defined in the sense of 'prayatne' (exertion, endeavor). By the rule 'shyan', it takes the class sign 'ya' in sarvadhatuka affixes, forming 'yasyati'. In combinations with prefixes such as 'pra' and 'a', it conveys striving (prayasa) and fatigue (ayasa) respectively.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'yasu prayatne' as exertion or purposeful activity (samiha). It forms 'yasyati' in the present tense and 'yayasa' in the perfect tense. Prefixed with 'an', it expresses fatigue (kheda) resulting from labor.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root snuh belongs to the 4th class (Divadigaṇa) and means to ooze, trickle, or drip. In the basic active form (Kartari), it takes the marker 'ya' (śyan) to become 'snuhyati', depicting a spontaneous trickling or flowing. When made causative with Nic (Prcchaka/Hetuman), it changes meaning to causing something to trickle, secrete, or discharge.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root shnuha is listed in the Divadigaṇa with the meaning prasravana (oozing, distilling, dripping). Initial retroflex sha converts to dental sa by 'dhatvadeh sah sah'. In the 4th class, it takes the shyan vikaraṇa yielding 'snuhyati'. By the sutra 'va druha-snuha-shniha-shnusham', it optionally takes it-agama in certain ardhadhatuka environments, showing dual forms in lit and lrt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines prasravanam as ksharanam or galanam (oozing, weeping, or trickling of liquids). It is classified as an anit root inherently, but allows optional it-agama in non-sarvadhatuka tenses. The forms proceed as snuhyati, sasnoha/susnoha, and snohita/snodha.

meanings.English: to ooze, to trickle, to flow out, to secrete

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhram' means to wander, roam around, or be dizzy/confused. When conjugated in the Divadi class (4th class), it takes the 'syan' marker and lengthens its vowel to form 'bhramyati'. In the causative form, adding 'nic' turns the meaning into 'making someone roam' or 'causing to spin/confuse', producing 'bhramayati'.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klam' means to become fatigued, exhausted, or to grow weary. Belongs to the 4th class (Divadi), it undergoes penultimate vowel lengthening in the present tense (forming 'klamyati' or 'klamyati' according to the sam-group rule 'samamastanang dirghah syani'). In its simple intransitive form, the subject itself experiences fatigue. When used with causative affixes (nic), it changes into a transitive verb meaning 'to exhaust or wear out someone else'.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'snih' means to feel love, fondness, or deep affection for someone, or physically to become smooth and unctuous. In the present tense, it takes the Divadi suffix '-ya-' to become 'snihyati'. The person or object toward whom affection is directed takes the locative (7th) or genitive (6th) case in Sanskrit. When used in the causative form with Nic ('snehayati'), it means to make someone affectionate or to lubricate.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya explains 'ṣṇiha prītau' as belonging to the Divadi group. By the rule 'dhatvadeh sah sah', initial dental 's' replaces cerebral 'sh'. It indicates emotional love (prema) as well as unctuousness. The regular present stem is formed with Shyan as 'snihyati', and it optionally admits It (Vet) in ardhadhatuka environments, giving past participle forms like 'snigdhaḥ'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'ṣṇiha prītau' that the primary semantic domain is emotional attachment (preti/anuraga) and physical stickiness or smoothness (snehavattvam). The Shyan suffix yields 'snihyati', and forms like 'sasneha' in Liti and 'snegdha/snehita' in Luti show its optional augment behavior.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tuṣ' belongs to the 4th conjugation (Divadi Gana) and means to be satisfied, contented, or pleased. In the present tense, it adds the class marker '-ya-' (śyan) to form 'tuṣyati'. When converted to a causative form (ṇijanta) as 'toṣayati', the meaning changes from experiencing satisfaction oneself to causing someone else to be pleased or satisfied.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'tuṣa tuṣṭau' is read in Divadi Gana in the sense of contentment and delight. It is an intransitive root taking Parasmaipada affixes with the Vikarana 'śyan'. As a member of the Radhādi subgroup, it optionally takes the augment 'iṭ' before valādi-ārdhadhātuka affixes (e.g., toṣitā / toṣṭā, tutoṣa, atoṣat / atuṣat).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses 'tuṣṭau' as 'tuṣṭiḥ prītiḥ' (pleasure or satisfaction). It takes Guna in strong Ārdhadhātuka contexts and forms 'tuṣyati' in Sārvadhātuka via Śyan without root vowel modification.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhram' means to wander, roam around, or be confused/unsteady. dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bus' means to discharge, release, shed, or cast away. When used with a causative affix (nic), it shifts meaning from becoming tranquil to actively subduing, taming, or controlling others as 'damayati'.
