vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'damu upasame' belongs to the Divadi gana and is anit and parasmaipadi. As part of the samadi group, it undergoes lengthening of the penultimate vowel by the sutra 'samamastanam dirghah syani' (7.3.74) before the affix syan, resulting in the form 'damyati'. In the causative, it forms 'damayati' through the application of the mit-marker rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin classifies 'damu upasame' among the eight roots of the samadi cluster within the Divadi class. It conveys the attainment of quietude, suppression of sensory passions (dama), or alleviation of agitation, undergoing radical vowel lengthening in the sarvadhatuka-syan environment.

meanings.English: to be tranquil, to exercise self-restraint, to tame or subdue
meanings.Kannada: upasanta agu, santa vagu, damana madu
meanings.Hindi: sant hona, indriya-daman karna, bas me karna
meanings.Bengali: santa howa, indriya daman kara, bose ana

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣībh' means to be intoxicated, ecstatic, excited, or careless (acting under intoxication or exuberance). In basic active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes the Divādi class marker '-ya-' to form 'kṣībhyati' (he/she becomes intoxicated or acts recklessly). When made causative (Nic-pratyaya), it becomes 'kṣebhayati', meaning to intoxicate or make someone careless.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), Divadi-shyan affix
scenarios.meaning: Becomes intoxicated or excited / acts heedlessly
scenarios.example_english: The man becomes intoxicated and careless through pride/wine.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat-lakara (present tense)
scenarios.meaning: Intoxicates or causes to become careless
scenarios.example_english: Pride intoxicates men.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṣībha' belongs to the Divadi gana with the semantic marker 'pramāde' (in the sense of intoxication, carelessness, or mental exhilaration). Taking the thematic affix 'śyan', it forms the present indicative base 'kṣībhya-' yielding 'kṣībhyati'. In ardhadhatuka forms, guna occurs optionally or obligatorily depending on affixal conditions.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kṣībha pramāde', equating 'pramāda' with loss of sobriety, intoxication, and negligence. It forms 'kṣībhyati' in the 4th class and produces derived nominals such as 'kṣība' or 'kṣībhita' (intoxicated).

meanings.English: to be intoxicated, to be excited, to be careless or negligent
meanings.Tamil: mattam aḍaital, kalitta iruttal, kavanakkuraivāy iruttal
meanings.Hindi: madmasta honā, matt honā, asāvadhāna honā
meanings.Bengali: matta haoyā, pramatta haoyā, osābadhāna haoyā
meanings.German: berauscht sein, trunken werden, unachtsam sein
meanings.French: être enivré, s'enivrer, être insouciant ou négligent

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kṣam belongs to the Divadi (4th) gana and is part of a special group of eight roots known as śamādi. Before the 4th-gana present tense suffix śyan (ya), its short vowel 'a' lengthens to long 'ā', giving the active present form kṣāmyati (he/she forgives or endures). In the causative (Nic) form, it becomes kṣamayati (causes to forgive or seeks pardon).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Divadi gana (śyan pratyaya with vowel lengthening by the rule śamāṃ aṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani)
scenarios.example_english: The virtuous person pardons all offenses.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya)
scenarios.meaning: Appeases, asks for forgiveness, or causes someone to forgive
scenarios.example_english: Having made a mistake, the student asks the teacher for forgiveness.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root kṣamū̃ sahane belongs to the Divadi class. As one of the eight roots in the śamādi grouping, it undergoes penultimate vowel lengthening in the presence of the śyan affix by the sutra 'śamāṃ aṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani' (Pāṇini 7.3.74), yielding kṣāmyati in the Parasmaipada present singular, distinguishing it from the Bhvadi Ātmanepada form kṣamate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines kṣamū̃ as 'sahane' denoting patience, tolerance (titikṣā), and pardon. He highlights the application of the śyan affix and the specific lengthened radical vowel yielding kṣāmyati, along with the standard unaugmented perfect and aorist derivations.

meanings.English: to endure, to tolerate, to forgive, to pardon
meanings.Bengali: sahyo kora, khoma kora, dhorjo dhora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tṛṣ' expresses the physiological condition or feeling of thirst. Falling in the Divadi class, it takes the class marker 'śyan' (-ya-) before Sarvadhatuka terminations, surfacing as 'tṛṣyati' in simple active present tense. When used in the causative (Nic), it shifts to active or dual-pada transitive usage 'tarṣayati' meaning 'to cause someone to thirst' or 'to parch'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (present indicative 3rd person singular with śyan pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: In the hot summer, the deer feels thirsty in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative present indicative 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The intense sunshine causes the traveler to become thirsty.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: tṛṣā pipāsāyām. divādiḥ parasmaipadī aniṭ. tṛṣyati, tatarṣa, tarṣitā/tarṣṭā, tarṣiṣyati/trakṣyati. śyani guṇābhāvaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: tṛṣā pipāsāyām. tṛṣyantīti śyan. ardhadhātuke 'tṛṣimṛṣikṛśeḥ kāśyapasya' iti seṭtva-vikalpaḥ smaryate.

meanings.English: to thirst, to be thirsty

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'puṣ' belongs to the 4th conjugation (Divādi-gaṇa) and means 'to nourish', 'to foster', or 'to thrive/grow strong'. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), the agent nourishes someone or thrives. When used with the causative affix (ṇic), it changes to mean 'causing someone to nourish or make thrive'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (Divādi śyan pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The mother nourishes the child with affection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic pratyaya (causative)
scenarios.example_english: The father fosters the trees with water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: puṣa puṣṭau. divādiḥ parasmaipadī aniṭ. puṣṭiḥ śarīrādi-upacayaḥ poṣaṇaṃ vā. śyani puṣyati iti rūpam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: puṣa puṣṭau. puṣyati, pupoṣa, poṣṭā, pukṣyati. upacaye vṛddhau ca vartate.

meanings.English: to nourish, foster, nurture, thrive
meanings.Bengali: poṣaṇa karā, lālan-pālan karā, puṣṭa haoẏā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sudh' means 'to become pure or clean'. In the 4th class (Divadi), it takes the marker '-ya-' to form 'sudhyati' (becomes pure). When we use the causative form (nic), it changes from 'becoming clean' to 'cleansing or purifying something else' as 'sodhayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Divadi-gana standard present tense (Kartari Lat, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: A person becomes pure after bathing in water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (Nich-pratyaya, Kartari Lat)
scenarios.example_english: Ganga water purifies a person.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'sudha sauce' belongs to the Divadi group and is intransitive (akarmaka) and unaugmented (anit). In Sarvadhatuka tenses, the class affix 'syan' is applied resulting in 'sudhyati'. In Ardhadhatuka tenses, Guna takes place before kit-free affixes, yielding forms like 'susodha' and 'soddha'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'sudha sauce' as an anit Divadi root denoting attainment of purity. It takes Parasmaipada endings systematically, forming 'sudhyati' in the present tense and 'asudhat' or 'asotsit' in the aorist.

meanings.English: to become pure, to be cleansed

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhram' means to wander, roam, rotate, or be confused. In the 4th class (Divadi), it optionally lengthens its vowel to 'bhrām-' before the class sign 'syan', giving two valid forms: 'bhramyati' and 'bhrāmyati'. When converted to a causative verb (Nich), it becomes 'bhrāmayati', meaning 'causes to spin' or 'leads astray'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Divadi-gana present tense (Lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The deer roams in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich-pratyaya (causative active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The boy spins the wheel.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'bhramu calane' is classified under Divadi-gana. By the sutra 'va bhrasa-bhlasa-bhramu-kramu-klamu-trasa-truti-lasam', the root vowel optionally undergoes dirgha (lengthening) in the presence of the syan pratyaya, resulting in bhrāmyati alongside bhramyati. In ardhadhatuka contexts, it admits optionally the it-agama according to rule.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'bhramu calane anavasthane ca'. It denotes wandering, instability, or unsteadiness. The forms bhrāmyati and bhramyati are standard in classical usage with optional lengthening in the fourth conjugation.

meanings.English: to wander, roam, spin, revolve, be confused
meanings.Chinese: you dang, xuan zhuan, mi huo

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'lī' belongs to the Divadi group and means 'to cling to', 'to hide into', or 'to dissolve/melt'. In simple present tense (kartari prayoga), it takes the Divadi suffix 'syan' (y) and Atmanepada endings to form 'līyate'. When combined with prefixes like 'vi', it means to dissolve or melt, and with 'ni' or 'sam', it means to hide or merge completely.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana (Divādi-gaṇa syan pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The child snuggles (clings lovingly) into the mother's lap.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: upasarga 'vi' + laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Salt dissolves completely in water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'līṅ śleṣaṇe' as an anit, Atmanepadi root of Divadi gana indicating adhering, merging, or dissolving. Under the Divadi class, it takes the 'syan' vikarana yielding 'līyate'. In the perfect tense (lit), reduplication produces 'lilye'. When used with preverbs like 'vi', it conveys liquefaction or melting.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini notes that 'līṅ' is used in the sense of embracing, clinging ('śleṣaṇa'), and disappearing or melting. He highlights its distinct conjugation across tenses, contrasting its primary Divadi present stem 'līyate' with secondary forms occurring across different upasarga combinations.

meanings.English: to cling, to adhere, to melt, to dissolve, to hide
meanings.Bengali: lepaṭe thākā, gola, lukiẏe thākā, bilīna haẏā
meanings.German: haften, sich schmiegen, schmelzen, sich auflösen

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root puṣ belongs to the 4th class (Divadi gana) and means to nourish, thrive, or foster. It takes the class sign -ya- (śyan) to form the base puṣya-, taking Parasmaipada endings. In active voice, it describes someone nourishing someone else or something flourishing. In the causative form (poṣayati), it emphasizes actively rearing or cultivating.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-puruṣa ekavacana with śyan vikaraṇa
scenarios.example_english: The mother nourishes the child with affection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative stem poṣi-), Lat-lakara, prathama-puruṣa ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The farmer fosters the crops with water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: puṣa puṣṭau. divādiḥ parasmaipadī aniṭ. śyan-vikaraṇe puṣyati iti rūpam sidhyati. puṣṭiḥ vṛddhiḥ upacayo vā ityarthaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: puṣa puṣṭau. puṣyati, pupoṣa. upacaye puṣṭiśabdaḥ vartate. aniṭ-lakṣaṇam sarvatra anugatam.

meanings.English: to nourish, to foster, to develop, to thrive

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tuṣ' belongs to the 4th class (Divādi) and means 'to be pleased, satisfied, or contented'. In its standard active form (tuṣyati), it shows the subject becoming happy on their own. When used with a causative affix (ṇic), it becomes 'toṣayati', meaning 'to please or satisfy someone else'. Adding upasargas like 'sam' (saṃtuṣyati) intensifies the sense of contentment.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Divādi-gaṇa (śyan pratyaya), Lat-lakāra, Prathama-puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy is pleased with the sweet.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya), Lat-lakāra, Prathama-puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The student pleases the teacher with good conduct.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'tuṣa tuṣṭau' is listed under the Divādi gaṇa. Taking the śyan vikarana, it forms 'tuṣyati'. The root denotes satisfaction or delight. In non-conjugational tenses, due to the ardhadhātuka rules and membership in the pushādi/svarādi series, it admits optional iṭ (veṭ) in forms like toṣiṣyati/tokṣyati and atoṣīt/atuṣat.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'tuṣa tuṣṭau' as denoting emotional contentment and gratification (prīti). Being an akarmaka root by nature, the cause of satisfaction is typically expressed in the instrumental (karaṇa/hetu) or locative case.

meanings.English: to be pleased, to be satisfied, to be contented

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sidh' means to succeed, be accomplished, or reach completion. In the basic Divadi active voice (sidhyati), the action happens naturally or as an outcome (a goal succeeds). When used with a causative affix (nic -> sadhayati), it transforms to mean actively achieving or accomplishing something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Divadi 4th Gana, Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice, Intransitive)
scenarios.example_sanskrit: Udyamena eva karyani sidhyanti na tu manorathaih.
scenarios.example_english: Tasks succeed solely through effort, not mere wishful thinking.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative, Transitive)
scenarios.example_english: The practitioner accomplishes perfection through truth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti classifies 'sidhu samsiddhau' under Divadigana as anit and parasmaipadi. It documents the derivation of present tense form 'sidhyati' with the 'syan' vikaranapratyaya, perfect 'sisedha', future 'setsyati', and past participle 'siddhah' formed under specific sandhi and elision rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'sidhu samsiddhau' as expressing the fruition, perfection, or successful materialization of an action or purpose. It distinguishes this root from the 1st gana 'sidha gati-nivrattau' (to ward off/restrain).

meanings.English: To succeed, to be accomplished, to attain fruition
meanings.Hindi: Siddha hona, saphal hona, poora hona
meanings.Bengali: Siddha howa, saphal howa, sampanna howa

canonical_dhatvartha: vidhyane (to pierce, to hit, to shoot, to wound)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vyadh' means to pierce, shoot, or strike a target. In the 4th conjugation (Divadi), it undergoes samprasarana (where 'vya' becomes 'vi') in sarvadhatuka tenses, resulting in forms like 'vidhyati'. When made causative, it means causing someone to pierce or shoot, conjugated as 'vyadhayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Divadi-gana (Syan pratyaya with Samprasarana), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/She pierces or strikes with an arrow
scenarios.example_english: The archer pierces the target with an arrow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to pierce or shoot
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the student to pierce the target.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'vyadha' belongs to Divadi-gana and has the meaning 'vidhyana' (vedhana / piercing). It takes the vikaranapratyaya 'Syan', which induces Samprasarana of 'vya' to 'vi' before kit/sarvadhatuka affixes, forming 'vidhyati'. In lit-lakara, reduplication yields 'vivyadha'. The root is anit and strictly Parasmaipadi in primary active voice.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'vyadha vidhyane tadane ca'. It belongs to the Divadi class. Due to the rule 'vyadhasya samprasaranam', it takes samprasarana before Syan and other applicable affixes, yielding forms such as 'vidhyati' and 'viddhah'.

meanings.English: to pierce, to shoot, to strike, to wound

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tras' means to be terrified, to tremble, or to be anxious. In the basic Divadi present tense (Kartari Prayoga), it uses the suffix 'Śyan' or optionally 'Śap' to mean 'becomes scared' (trasyati / trasati). When you use the causative form (Nic pratyaya), it becomes transitive ('trasayati'), meaning 'frightens' or 'scares' someone else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Divādi Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense 3rd Person Singular with Śyan)
scenarios.example_english: The deer is afraid of the lion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Ṇic Pratyaya (Causative Present Tense 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The tiger frightens the animals.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'trasī' belongs to the Divādigaṇa and is defined in the sense of 'udvega' (agitation, fear, trembling). Under the sutra 'vā trāsa-bhrama-kṣamā-klamā-masām' (P. 3.1.70), it optionally takes the vikaraṇa 'Śap' alongside the regular 'Śyan', producing forms like 'trasyati' and 'trasati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'trasī udvege' denotes mental perturbation or physical trembling caused by fear. Its 'ir-it' nature permits the optional insertion of ṛ/aṅ forms in past tenses, and it takes optional vikarana in kartari present system.

meanings.English: to be afraid, to tremble, to fear, to be agitated

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'as' means to throw, shoot, or cast. As a Class 4 (Divadi) verb, it adds the marker '-ya-' in the present tense to form 'asyati' (he/she throws). When combined with prefixes (upasargas), its meaning changes vividly: with 'nir-' it means 'to expel or dispel', and with 'sam-' it means 'to assemble or compound'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The brave warrior shoots an arrow towards the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: upasarga 'nir' + lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The rising sun dispels all darkness.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: asu ksepe. divadih parasmaipadi anit sakarmakah. asyati, asa, asita/asta, asisyati. ksepanam preranam ityarthah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: asu ksepe. asyati banam. upasargavasad vividharthata yatha nirastah, samastah, vyastah ityadi.

meanings.English: to throw, cast, shoot, project, discharge

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kus' belongs to the Divadi class (4th conjugation) and takes the suffix 'syan' (-ya-) in the present tense, giving the form 'kusyati'. It means to extract, draw out, or pull out something from within. When used in causative (Nic), it forms 'kosayati', meaning to cause someone to extract or peel.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The doctor extracts the splinter from the wound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The farmer causes the servant to extract the seed from the fruit.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kusu nishkarshe. Divadir anudatted anudattopadeshah. Nishkarshah prithakkaranam vislesho va. Kusyati, cukosa, kosita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kusu nishkarshe. Nishkarshanam akarshanam vishleshana-purvakam prithak-karanam. Kusyati, kosishyati, akosit.

meanings.English: to extract, to draw out, to pull apart

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tam' belongs to the Divadi group (4th class) and denotes becoming exhausted, fainting, choking, or longing deeply. Because it takes the fourth-conjugation affix 'syan', its vowel lengthens to form 'tāmyati' in the basic present tense. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it shifts meaning to causing someone to become exhausted, distressed, or breathless (tamayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular with syan-vikarana and vowel lengthening
scenarios.example_english: The traveler faints due to the scorching hot wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Hetumati Nic (causative active), Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The excessive load exhausts the child.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: tamū kāṅkṣāyām. anit parasmaipadī. 'śama-tam-adām aṣṭānām dīrghaḥ śyani' iti dīrghatve prāpte tāmyati iti rūpam sidhyati. kāṅkṣā glāniśca asyārthaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: tamū kāṅkṣāyām glānau ca. divādiranit. tāmyati, tatāma, tāntā. 'tam khedane' ityanye.

meanings.English: to be exhausted, to faint, to languish, to desire or long for
meanings.Bengali: klanta hawa, murchha jawa, apeksha ba aakanksha kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tras' means to fear, tremble, or become agitated with anxiety. In the Divadi group, it takes the marker 'syan' (-ya-) to form 'trasyati' in the active voice (Parasmaipada). When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it changes to 'trāsayati', which means 'to frighten' or 'to cause someone to tremble with fear'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Divadi vikarana (syan)
scenarios.example_english: The deer is frightened of the lion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The tiger terrifies everyone.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: trasi udvege. Divadi parasmaipadi anit. Udvegah bhayam kampo va. Syan-vikaranena trasyati iti rupam sidhyati. Trasadeh ac-pratyaye trasah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: trasi udvege. Trasate trasyati va iti ganabhedat. Divadau syan trasyati. Udvegah cittasambhrmah bhayam ca.

meanings.English: to tremble, to fear, to be agitated, to be terrified

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rup' belongs to the 4th conjugation (Divadi gana) and takes the class sign 'syan' (ya) before endings. It expresses confounding, bewildering, or disturbing mentally. In the standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent experiencing or causing state of confusion or disturbance. When used with causative affix (nic), it means to cause someone to become thoroughly confused or distressed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha (3rd person), ekavacana (singular), kartari prayoga (active voice)
scenarios.meaning: Becomes bewildered or suffers mental confusion
scenarios.example_english: The kind-hearted person becomes disturbed due to delusion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The crooked argument perplexes the person.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'rupa vimohane' is classified under Divadi gana. In Sarvadhatuka tenses, the vikaranapratyaya 'syan' is applied resulting in 'rupyati'. The dhatu conveys the sense of delusion, deep confusion, or breaking/disturbing mental equilibrium (vimohana). Perfect tense forms 'ruropa' and causative 'ropayati' follow regular gunadi rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin groups 'yupa', 'rupa', and 'lupa' together under the sense of 'vimohane'. Here 'rupa' denotes confounding, being bewildered, or causing stupor. Forms include 'rupyati', 'ruropa', 'ropita'.

meanings.English: to be bewildered, to confound, to disturb, to suffer stupor
meanings.Hindi: vimohit hona, bhramit hona, vyakul hona
meanings.French: etre deconcerte, etre trouble, etre plonge dans la stupeur
meanings.Russian: prihodit v zameshatelstvo, byt omrachennym, teryat golovu

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kṛś means to become thin, weak, or emaciated. In standard 4th class active usage (Parasmaipada with the 'śyan' suffix), it describes someone or something naturally losing weight or body mass. When used in causative (ṇijanta), it changes to mean causing someone or something to become thin or emaciating through austere practices or lack of nourishment.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular with Divadi vikaranai śyan.
scenarios.example_english: The ascetic becomes thin due to illness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative stem) in Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, 3rd person singular.
scenarios.meaning: Causes to become thin, emaciates or weakens.
scenarios.example_english: Severe austerity emaciates the body.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṛśa tanūkaraṇe' belongs to the Divādi class and is Parasmaipadi and Aniṭ. In Sarvadhatuka tenses, the affix śyan is applied yielding kṛśyati. The meaning 'tanūkaraṇa' denotes reduction of bodily bulk or becoming slender.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kṛśa tanūkaraṇe' as an Aniṭ root of the Divādi group. It forms kṛśyati in the present system, cakṛśa in the perfect (Lit), and shows vṛddhi/guṇa adjustments in causative forms like karśayati.

meanings.English: to become lean, to grow thin, to emaciate
meanings.Bengali: kṛśa haoyā, śukīye jāoyā, rogā haoyā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dam' means to practice self-restraint, to become calm, or to be subdued. In Gana 4 (Divadi), it lengthens its internal 'a' vowel to 'a' before the present stem affix (syan), forming 'damyati'. When made causative with Nic, it means to tame or subdue someone else ('damayati').

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Gana 4 divadi-syan with stem lengthening)
scenarios.example_english: The ascetic practices self-control in the penance grove.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Kartari Prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The king subdues the enemies.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: damu upaśame. Divādiḥ parasmaipadī aniṭ. 'śamām aṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani' iti dīrghatve prāpte 'dāmyati' iti rūpaṃ bhavati. Dāntaḥ, damitā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: damu upaśame. Upaśamo dānto bhāvaḥ indriyasaṃyamaḥ. Dāmyati, dāntaḥ, damanaḥ. Śamāditvāt dīrghaḥ.

meanings.English: to be tamed, to practice self-restraint, to become quiet or calm
meanings.Hindi: shaant hona, indriyon ko vash me karna, sanyam rakhna
meanings.Bengali: indriya samyama kora, shanto howa, daman kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śuṣ' belongs to the 4th class (Divadi) and naturally takes Parasmaipada endings with the 'ya' suffix (śyan) to mean 'to dry up' or 'to wither'. When the causative suffix (Nic) is added, it transitions from intransitive to transitive, meaning 'to make dry' or 'to desiccate'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Divadi Class 4 kartari prayoga (active voice with śyan pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The tree withers without water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The sun dries up the water of the lake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: śuṣa śoṣaṇe. divādir aniṭ parasmaipadī. śuṣyati, śuṣoṣa, śoṣṭā, śokṣyati. niṣṭhāyāṃ 'śuṣaḥ kaḥ' iti katve śuṣkaḥ iti rūpam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: śuṣa śoṣaṇe. śuṣyati. śuṣoṣa. śuṣkaḥ ityatra niṣṭhātasya katvam.

meanings.English: to dry up, wither, become arid

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śliṣ' belongs to the 4th conjugation group (Divādi gaṇa) and primarily denotes embracing, adhering, or clinging to someone or something. In the present tense, it takes the class sign 'śyan' (-ya-) to form 'śliṣyati'. When combined with the causative suffix 'ṇic', it becomes 'śleṣayati', meaning to cause to adhere, join together, or connect.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (Divadi shyan pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The mother embraces the child with affection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The craftsman joins the wooden pieces together.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'śliṣa āliṅgane' under Divadi gaṇa as taking the vikaraṇa 'śyan' in kartari prayoga, resulting in the form 'śliṣyati'. It highlights that the radical vowel remains un-lengthened (no guna) in the presence of sarvadhatuka 'śyan', preserving the short 'i' base.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'śliṣa āliṅgane' that this root denotes embracing, contact, or intimate cohesion. In non-conjugational tenses without 'śyan', regular guṇa changes apply depending on the pratyaya nature, maintaining its classification as an aniṭ root.

meanings.English: to embrace, clasp, cling, or adhere to

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vyadh' means to pierce, shoot, or strike with a weapon. When we form the present tense in the fourth verb class (Divadi gana), the infix 'ya' (syan) triggers a vowel change called Samprasarana where 'vya' turns into 'vi', giving forms like 'vidhyati' (he/she pierces or shoots). In the causative form with 'nic', it means 'causes to be pierced or shot' (vyadhayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular with samprasarana change
scenarios.example_english: The archer pierces the target with an arrow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the student to pierce the target.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'vyadha tadane' belongs to Divadi gana and is Parasmaipadi and Anit. In Sarvadhatuka environments with the syan pratyaya, Samprasarana is applied by the sutra 'grahi-jya-vayi-vyadhi-vashti-vicati-vrscati-prcchati-bhrjjatinam niti ca' resulting in the base 'vidhya-', giving the present form 'vidhyati'. In perfect tense (Lit), it forms 'vivyadha' with reduplication and vowel restoration.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'vyadha tadane' as an Anit root of the Divadi class. Its core semantic denotes piercing, wounding, or striking with weapons. The stem becomes 'vidhya-' before Kit and Nit affixes due to regular samprasarana rules, and takes the passive form 'vidhyate'.

meanings.English: to pierce, to strike, to shoot, to wound
meanings.Hindi: bhedna, chhedna, ban marna, prahar karna
meanings.French: transpercer, percer, frapper d une fleche

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'snih' means 'to feel affection', 'to love', or 'to be fond of'. Being in the 4th conjugation (Divadi), it receives the 'ya' (syan) affix to form the basic active stem 'snihyati'. The person who is loved is typically placed in the locative (saptami) or accusative (dvitiya) case. When using the causative suffix (nic), it becomes 'snehayati', meaning 'to make fond of' or 'to treat with affection'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana with syan pratyaya
scenarios.example_english: The mother always feels affection for her children.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to love / treats tenderly with love
scenarios.example_english: The teacher treats the students with loving affection.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ṣṇiha prītau. anit, para-smai-bhāṣā. śyan-vikaraṇaḥ. prītiḥ prema-rūpo bhāvaḥ. snihyati, sasneha, snekṣyati, asnāhīt/asnihat ityādīni rūpāṇi.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ṣṇiha prītau. 'dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ' iti sakāraḥ, 'no naḥ' iti nakāraḥ. snihyati, snigdhaḥ, snehaḥ ityādi sādhayati.

meanings.English: to love, to feel affection, to be fond of, to be smooth or unctuous
meanings.Telugu: premincuta, snehamu ceyuta, anuragamu kaligi yunduta
meanings.Hindi: sneh karna, prem karna, lagav rakhna
meanings.Bengali: bhalobasha, sneh kora, anurag poshon kora
meanings.Russian: lyubit, ispytyvat privyazannost, otnositsya s lyubovyu
meanings.Chinese: ai, xi ai, huai you ai qing

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svid' belongs to the 4th conjugation (Divadi gana) and takes the 'syan' affix (giving -ya-) in the present tense to form 'svidyati'. It primarily denotes the natural bodily process of perspiring or sweating due to heat, physical exertion, or fear. When used in the causative (Nic), it shifts to 'svedayati', meaning to cause someone to sweat, or in Ayurveda, to apply steam/sudation therapy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Present tense (Lat lakara), Parasmaipada, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: Due to the heat, the farmer sweats profusely in the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Present tense
scenarios.meaning: causes to sweat / applies heat therapy
scenarios.example_sanskrit: vaidyah roginam aushadhair ushnena cha svedayati.
scenarios.example_english: The physician induces perspiration in the patient with warm medicinal therapies.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'ṣvidā gātrasmsvede' as a root where the initial dental 'sa' replaces the aupadeshika cerebral 'ṣa' (dhatvadeh sah sah). It takes the Divadi vikarana 'syan' in Sarvadhatuka forms, producing 'svidyati'. In Ardhadhatuka environments like the perfect (Lit), it yields 'siṣveda', and optionally admits It-agama depending on specific affixal constraints.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'ṣvidā gātrasmsvede' specifically indicates exudation from the body pores caused by inner heat, labor, or apprehension. It aligns in morphological behavior with roots like 'klid' and 'kshvid', forming 'svinna' with the past participle suffix 'kta' by the phonological rule converting the dental stop to 'na' and causing assimilation.

meanings.English: to sweat, to perspire

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root piṣ belongs to the 4th Gana (Divādi) and takes the vikaraṇa affix 'śyan' (-ya-) in standard active forms to convey aggregation, collecting together, or pounding/striking together. In the causative (ṇijanta), it conveys causing something to be aggregated or crushed together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakāra, Divādi śyan vikaraṇa, Parasmaipada, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: aggregates, collects together, or impacts together
scenarios.example_english: The person joins together in a crowd.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇijanta), Lat lakāra, Parasmaipada, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to collect or causes to crush together
scenarios.example_english: The organizer brings the people together.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: piṣa saṅghāte - divādir anit parasmaibhāṣā. śyani piṣyatīti rūpam. piṣa saṅghāte ityatra saṅghātaḥ saṅgrahaḥ samavāyo vā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: piṣa saṅghāte. piṣyati. pipeṣa. pekṣyati. anit. saṅghāte samavāye ca vartate.

meanings.English: to aggregate, to assemble, to bring or strike together

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root klam means to become tired, fatigued, or exhausted. Belonging to the Divadi class, it takes the class marker shyan (-ya-). A special rule lengthens the short vowel 'a' to long 'a', producing the present form 'klamyati' (he/she becomes weary). When used with a causative suffix, it shifts from an intransitive sense to a transitive one, meaning 'to exhaust or wear out someone else'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The traveler becomes weary from the long road.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The intense heat exhausts the farmer.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti classifies klamu in the sense of glani (fatigue/decline). Under Panini sutra 'shamamashtanam dirghah shyani' (7.3.74), the root undergoes penultimate vowel lengthening in the presence of shyan, yielding the form klamyati. The past participle form is formed as klanta through standard phonological rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes klamu as belonging to the samadi group under the Divadi class. It conveys bodily exhaustion or mental weariness (glani), undergoing stem lengthening before shyan to form klamyati.

meanings.English: to become fatigued, to grow weary, to languish

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ris' means to steal, plunder, or cause harm/destruction to someone or something. Being a Divadi gana root, it takes the class marker 'syan' (-ya-) in simple present tense active voice, forming 'risyati'. When causative suffix (Nic) is added, it forms 'resayati', which means to cause someone to steal or cause injury/loss to another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusa, ekavacana with syan pratyaya
scenarios.example_english: The thief robs (steals from) the wealthy person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative stem), Lat lakara, prathama purusa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The master does not cause the servant to steal or cause harm.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The author notes 'risa steye' under the Divadi class. It conjugates with 'syan' affix yielding 'risyati'. Being anit in nature with a penultimate 'i' vowel, it takes guna in non-sarvadhatuka environments where applicable (e.g., aresit in Lun), indicating the action of illicit acquisition (stealing) or harming.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin identifies 'risa' as conveying 'steya' (theft/robbery) and 'himsa' (injury/destruction). It shares conjugational behavior with other sibilant-final Divadi roots, forming 'risyati' in the present indicative Parasmaipada.

meanings.English: To steal, rob, injure, or cause damage
meanings.Bengali: churi kara, apaharan kara, khoti kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klis' means to suffer, experience distress, or be tormented. In the 4th conjugation (Divadi gana), it takes the Vikarana affix 'syan' (ya) to form 'klisyati' in Parasmaipada, describing someone undergoing affliction or pain. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it changes into 'kleshayati', meaning 'to cause someone to suffer' or 'to torment someone'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 4th gana Vikarana 'syan'
scenarios.example_english: The body of the sick person suffers affliction.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The intense heat torments the traveler.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti records 'klisa upatape' under Divadi, yielding 'klisyati'. The root denotes suffering, torment, and distress. In ardhadhatuka forms, it optionally admits the augment it by the rule 'ardhadhatukasya it valadeh' along with contextual optionality (vet-tva).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'klis' signifies experiencing mental or physical affliction ('upatapah pidanam'). He distinguishes the fourth-class formation 'klisyati' from the ninth-class formation 'klisnati' (Kryadi), highlighting standard phonological mutations and optional it in past participles (klistah/kleshitas).

meanings.English: to suffer, to be distressed, to torment
meanings.Kannada: novannu anubhavisu, sankatakke olagagu, klesha hondu
meanings.Hindi: kashta pana, dukhi hona, klesha anubhava karna
meanings.Bengali: kosto pawa, dukho bhog kora, klesh pawa
meanings.French: souffrir, etre tourmente, endurer une peine

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'puṣ' belongs to the 4th class (Divadigaṇa) and fundamentally means to nourish, thrive, grow, or sustain. In the standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent nourishing someone or thriving. When converted into the causative form (nic), it means to cause someone to nourish, foster, or rear.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (Divadi - śyan pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The mother nourishes the child with milk.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to be nourished / sustains / fosters
scenarios.example_english: The king fosters the citizens through righteousness.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root puṣa~ takes the vikarana śyan in the Divadigaṇa and signifies bodily nourishment, flourishing, or growth (puṣṭau). Being aniṭ in general conjugations, it forms puṣyati, pupoṣa, poṣṭā, and puṣyāt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'puṣa puṣṭau' signifies development, enrichment, and sustenance. In the fourth class, it takes the class marker śyan without guna in sarvadhatuka affixes, forming puṣyati.

meanings.English: to nourish, foster, rear, thrive, grow
meanings.Hindi: poshana karna, palan-poshan karna, pushta hona
meanings.Bengali: poshon kora, palon kora, pushto howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mā' (with marker 'ṅ') belongs to the 4th class (Divādi). It adds the middle infix '-ya-' (śyan) to express measuring, assessing, or sizing something. Because it carries an 'ṅ' marker (ṅit), it uses only Ātmanepada (middle voice) endings in its basic form.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakāra (present tense), 3rd person singular with śyan vikarana
scenarios.example_english: The artisan measures the timber with a measuring rod.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Ṇijanta), Lat lakāra, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to measure / has surveyed or constructed
scenarios.example_english: The owner has the field measured by the worker.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: māṅ māne. Divāditvāt śyan. Ātmanepadī anit sakarmakaśca. māyate, mame, mātā, māsyate ityādīni rūpāṇi sidhyanti. Parimāṇe arthaviśeṣe ca vartate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: māṅ māne. Mānaṃ paricchedaḥ parimāṇaṃ vā. Śyanā māyate. Ātmanepada-ekāntaḥ.

meanings.English: to measure, to mete out, to quantify

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tus' means 'to be satisfied' or 'to be pleased'. As a 4th class (Divadi) root, it adds '-ya-' (syan) between the root and verb ending in the present tense, remaining in Parasmaipada (tusyati). When used with a causative affix (Nic), it shifts to the meaning 'to please' or 'to satisfy' someone else (tosayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Divadi-gana Kartari prayoga (syan pratyaya, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The sage is satisfied with fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The boy pleases his father by good work.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti categorizes 'tusa tustau' in Divadigana with syan affix. It undergoes samprasarana-like avoidance of guna before sarvadhatuka syan giving 'tusyati'. In lit lakara, it forms 'tutosa', and the past passive participle yields 'tustah' via regular dental-to-retroflex sandhi rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'tustau' as synonymous with 'pritau' (delight or contentment). It is noted as an anit root, forming forms like 'tosta' in lut and 'tustah' with kta pratyaya without intermediate it-agama.

meanings.English: to be satisfied, to be pleased, to rejoice
meanings.Hindi: santusht hona, prasanna hona, tript hona
meanings.Bengali: santushta haoya, khushi haoya, tripta haoya
meanings.German: zufrieden sein, sich freuen, befriedigt werden
meanings.French: etre satisfait, se contenter, se rejouir

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dī' belongs to the 4th class (Divādi) and means to fly or glide through the sky. Because it has an indicatory letter 'ṅ' (dīṅ), it takes Ātmanepada endings in standard conjugation. In the present tense, the Divādi vikaraṇa 'śyan' (-ya-) is added, yielding the basic form 'dīyate'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The bird flies in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Bahuvacana (plural)
scenarios.meaning: they fly / they soar in the sky
scenarios.example_english: The birds soar in the sky.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dīṅ vihāyasā gatau. anit, ātmanepadī. vihāyasaḥ ākāśaḥ, tatra gamanamityarthaḥ. śyani dīyate iti rūpam sidhyati. liṭi didīye.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dīṅ vihāyasā gatau. vihāyasaḥ ākāśaḥ, tatra gatiḥ patanam uḍḍayanam vā. dīyate pakṣī.

meanings.English: to fly, to soar through the sky, to glide

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'as' belongs to the 4th class (Divadi gana) and carries the core meaning of throwing, casting, or shooting. When conjugated in active voice with the 'syan' marker (y), it takes Parasmaipada endings to mean 'throws'. With upasargas (prefixes) like 'pra' (prasyati) or 'nir' (nirasvati/nirasyati), it nuances the action toward casting forward or expelling.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The archer shoots an arrow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'nir' + Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The scholar dispels the doubt.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'asu kshepane' as an anit Divadi Parasmaipada root. In sarvadhatuka tenses, it takes the class marker 'syan' yielding the base 'asya-'. The root forms 'asyati' in the present tense. In ardhadhatuka forms, elision and sandhi operations follow standard Paninian rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'asu kshepane' under Divadi, emphasizing the semantic boundary of forceful projection (kshepana) in contrast to mere placing (nyasa). It regularly forms 'asyati', 'asa', and 'asita/asta' in relevant participial and perfect paradigms.

meanings.English: to throw, cast, shoot, direct towards

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mī' belongs to the 4th class (Divadi gana) and means to harm, hurt, or destroy. In the present tense, it takes the class sign 'ya' to become 'mīyati'. It is used in the active voice (Parasmaipada) when a subject causes injury or harm directly to an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Divadi śyan affix
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person always harms an innocent person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya), Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the enemy to be destroyed by the soldier.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mī' is classified under Divadigana in the sense of violence and injury (hiṃsāyām). It takes the Parasmaipada affixes and is anit. With the śyan vikaraṇa, it yields the form 'mīyati'. In perfect tense (lit), it forms 'mamau' or 'mimāya'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin lists 'mī hiṃsāyām' as an anit Parasmaipada root denoting harming, killing, or impairing (hiṃsana/vadha), showing regular derivation with śyan in sarvadhatuka contexts as 'mīyati'.

meanings.English: to injure, to harm, to destroy, to kill
meanings.Hindi: hiṃsā karnā, choṭ pahuñcānā, naṣṭ karnā
meanings.Bengali: hiṃsā karā, āghāt karā, binaṣṭa karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hṛṣ' primarily means to rejoice, to be thrilled, or for the body hairs to bristle/stand on end due to intense delight or chill. When used in standard Divadi present tense, it takes the class-marker 'syan' (ya) yielding 'hṛṣyati'. In the causative (nic) form, it turns into 'harṣayati', meaning 'to cause someone to rejoice' or 'to gladden'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Divadi (śyan) Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy rejoices upon receiving the award.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: Sweet speech gladdens the mind of everyone.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The author notes hṛṣa with the meaning of tuṣṭi (joy, satisfaction) as well as pratighāta (horripilation, bristling of hair due to joy, fear, or cold). Being a root of the Divadi class, it takes the affix 'śyan' in the active voice, producing the present stem 'hṛṣya-'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains that 'hṛṣa tuṣṭipratighātayoḥ' applies to emotional exultation as well as physiological reactions like romāñca (hair-raising thrill). Its primary finite paradigms in the present tense remain Parasmaipada.

meanings.English: to rejoice, to exult, to bristle with joy
meanings.Hindi: harṣita honā, prasanna honā, romāñcita honā
meanings.Bengali: ānandita haoẏā, harṣita haoẏā, romāñcita haoẏā
meanings.German: sich freuen, frohlocken, vor Freude erschauern
meanings.French: se réjouir, frémir de joie, jubiler

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klam' belongs to the 4th class (Divadi-gana) and means to become tired, fatigued, or exhausted. Because it belongs to the special 'samadi' group, its vowel lengthens to 'a' in the present tense with the 'syan' (ya) suffix, forming 'klamyati'. In the causative (nic), it takes the meaning of causing someone to become weary or exhausting someone ('klamayati').

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular with syan-pratyaya (lengthening by samam astanam dirghah syani)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler becomes weary due to the long path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat-lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The intense heat exhausts the farmer.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'klamu glanau' is placed in the Divadi-gana. It is an akarmaka root signifying loss of physical energy, dejection, or languor. By the sutra 'samam astanam dirghah syani' (7.3.74), the penultimate vowel 'a' undergoes lengthening before the 'syan' vikarana in the sarvadhatuka present tense, resulting in the form 'klamyati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'klamu glanau' within the samadi sub-class of the fourth conjugation. It denotes 'glani' (physical or mental exhaustion). In non-syan environments and krdanta forms, variations like 'klamyati', 'klantah', or 'klamitah' occur as per Paninian rules.

meanings.English: to grow weary, to become fatigued, to exhaust

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dāś' belongs to the 4th class (Divadi) and means to give, bestow, or make an offering. In the active voice (Kartari), it takes the marker 'ya' (śyan) to form 'dāśyati'. In the passive voice (Karmani), it takes Atmanepada endings with 'yak' to express that something is being bestowed or offered.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Active Voice), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The devotee offers the sacred oblation to the deity.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Karmani prayoga (Passive Voice), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: is given / is bestowed / is offered
scenarios.example_english: A charitable gift is bestowed upon the wise man by the donor.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dāśu dāne. divādiḥ parasmaipadī seṭ. dāne arthe vartate. śyanipratyaye dāśyati iti rūpam. dāśitā, dāśiṣyati. diśādyanit-parigaṇane asyānuktatvāt seṭtvam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dāśu dāne. dāśyati, dadāśa. dānam arpaṇam utsargo vā. seṭ.

meanings.English: to give, to bestow, to offer, to grant

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'as' means to throw, shoot, or cast an object. In Class 4 (Divadi), it adds the middle infix '-ya-' (śyan) to form the base 'asya-'. When used in active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent actively hurling, throwing, or discharging an object such as an arrow or a stone. Adding prefixes (upasargas) like 'nir' alters the meaning to 'throwing out' or 'banishing'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra (present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior shoots an arrow at the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: upasarga 'nir' + kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra
scenarios.example_english: The king expels the wicked man from the city.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'asu kṣepe' as expressing the act of throwing, propelling, or discharging (kṣepaṇa/preraṇa). Belonging to the divādi class, it takes the vikaraṇa 'śyan' yielding 'asyati'. In the past participle form, it drops the radical 's' before 'ta' to yield 'asta' (cast/thrown/set).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'asu' in the primary sense of projectile motion and casting away. Derived terms like 'astra' (a missile weapon that is thrown or discharged) and 'nirasa' (rejection or removal) are directly formed from this root under relevant Paninian unadi and kridanta affixes.

meanings.English: to throw, cast, shoot, hurl

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'as' belongs to the 4th class (Divadi gana) and carries the basic sense of throwing, hurling, or shooting. In the present tense, it receives the 'syan' affix (-ya-), producing forms like 'asyati' (he/she throws). When used with causative affixes (nic), it signifies inducing or directing someone to throw an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Syan vikarana)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior shoots an arrow towards the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to throw / makes one launch
scenarios.example_english: The commander makes the soldiers hurl their weapons.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: asu ksepe. divadih parasmaipadi anit. syani asyati. aso nu hy asamyogalighoh iti sutrena nut pravartate kintu halanta-prakriyayam niyamah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: asu ksepe. asyati, asa, asta, asisyati. ksepanam preranam ityetadarthakah.

meanings.English: to throw, cast, hurl, shoot, or project

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣībh' belongs to the 4th conjugation (Divadi gana) and expresses being intoxicated, excited, or reeling from passion or drink. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it adds the affix 'ya' (śyan) to yield forms like 'kṣībhyati'. When expressing a causative sense (making someone intoxicated or excited), it takes the 'ṇic' affix to form 'kṣebhayati' or 'kṣībhayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular with Divadi 'syan' vikarana
scenarios.example_english: The man becomes intoxicated by liquor.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: Wine inebriates that man.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kṣībhā made - divādiḥ parasmaipadī seṭ. kṣībhyati, cikṣībha, kṣībhitā, kṣībhiṣyati. madaḥ harṣaḥ mattatā vā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kṣībhā made - kṣībhyatīti syan. kṣebhana-arthatvāt madasyābhivyaktiḥ. bhraśādi-sūtreṇa vikalpitā vidhayaḥ.

meanings.English: to be intoxicated, to reel, to be excited or drunk

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dṛp' belongs to the 4th group (Divadi-gana) and means to become proud, arrogant, foolishly overjoyed, or intoxicated with pride. In the simple active present tense (Kartari Prayoga), it takes the fourth-class suffix 'syan' (-ya-) to form 'dṛpyati'. When adding the causative suffix (Nic), it becomes 'darpayati' (makes someone proud or inflates their ego).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Divadi class marker (syan)
scenarios.meaning: Becomes arrogant or intoxicated with pride
scenarios.example_english: The foolish person becomes arrogant due to wealth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara
scenarios.meaning: Causes pride or inflates the ego of another
scenarios.example_english: The acquisition of worthless wealth inflates the ill-natured man's ego.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dṛpa harṣamohanayoḥ' is listed under the Divadi class. It denotes exhilaration (harṣa) and delusion or arrogance (mohana). Being in Divadi, it receives the 'śyan' vikarana yielding forms like 'dṛpyati'. It is optionally 'iṭ' (vet) in ārdhadhātuka affixes.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'dṛpa harṣamohanayoḥ' as a fourth-class root representing excessive intoxication through pride or foolish joy. Perfect stem forms exhibit alternate guṇa and vṛddhi configurations according to relevant sutras.

meanings.English: to be proud, to become arrogant, to rejoice foolishly, to be intoxicated with pride
meanings.Tamil: karvam kolvathu, thimiru kolluthal, magizhchi adaivathu
meanings.Hindi: ghamand karna, garvit hona, madmast hona
meanings.Bengali: gorbo kora, ohoṅkrito howa, ullasito howa
meanings.German: stolz sein, uberheblich werden, berauscht sein

canonical_dhatvartha: himsayam (in the sense of injuring, harming, or destroying)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root ksap belongs to the 4th group (Divadi gana) and takes the parasmaipada endings. It adds the infix -ya- to form the present base 'ksapya-'. It means to hurt, destroy, or injure. When used in the causative (Nic), it takes the form 'ksapayati', meaning to cause to destroy or to exhaust.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana (divadi yak-pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior destroys the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: He/she causes to destroy or wear down
scenarios.example_english: The ascetic destroys sins through austerity.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'kshapa himsayam' under the Divadi-gana with parasmaipada inflection. As an anit root, it forms the present tense base 'ksapyati' using the shyan affix without vowel lengthening in the unaugmented state.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'kshapa' denotes injury, casting down, or ruin ('himsayam'). It follows standard Divadi rules taking yak (shyan), yielding forms like kshapyati, akshapyat, and chaksapa in the perfect.

meanings.English: to injure, harm, destroy, or strike down
meanings.Hindi: hinsa karna, vinash karna, nasht karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root klid belongs to the 4th conjugation (Divadi gana) and takes the suffix -ya- (syan) in the present tense to mean 'to become wet' or 'to rot/putrefy by dampness'. It is intransitive in its base form (klidyati), but when made causative with nic (kledayati), it becomes transitive and means 'to moisten' or 'to make wet'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Base form (Divadi Parasmaipada with syan pratyaya)
scenarios.meaning: Becomes wet / moistens on its own
scenarios.example_english: The cloth becomes wet in the rainwater.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (nic pratyaya)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to become wet / moistens something
scenarios.example_english: The farmer moistens the seed with water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes niklida ardribhave in the Divadi class. The initial anubandha 'ni' indicates that the root takes the kta affix in the sense of the beginning of action (adikarma). Being in the Divadi gana, it takes the syan vikarana yielding klidyati. In the perfect tense (lit), it forms cikleda by regular guna without am-pratyaya.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini glosses klid as ardribhava (the state of becoming moist, wet, or softened by liquid). It notes the anit status in ardhadhatuka environments, distinguishing it from roots of similar phonetic shape in other classes.

meanings.English: to become wet, to be moist, to soften by moisture

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rdh' means to prosper, grow, or thrive. In its basic 4th class form (Divadi), it takes the marker 'syan' and Parasmaipada endings to mean thriving naturally. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it changes meaning to 'making someone or something prosper or grow'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Divadi gana with syan pratyaya in Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The kingdom prospers through righteousness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The king makes the country prosper.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: rdha vriddhau. Divadi-gana Parasmaipadi anit. Syani prapte rdhyati iti rupam siddhyati. Vriddhavarthe ayam vartate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: rdha vriddhau. Syana rdhyati. Svadi-pathat rdhnoti iti api rupam bhavati bhedena.

meanings.English: to grow, to prosper, to thrive, to succeed
meanings.Bengali: briddhi paoya, samriddha haoya, unnati kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dīṅ' belongs to the 4th class (Divādi) and takes the Ātmanepada endings. It uses the infix 'ya' (śyan) to form its present tense base 'dīyate', meaning 'to decay', 'to waste away', or 'to diminish'. When used with prefixes or causatives, the action describes causing reduction or destruction.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lat-lakāra (present indicative), prathama-puruṣa eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: With the passage of time, bodily strength diminishes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇijanta (causative), parasmaipada, lat-lakāra
scenarios.meaning: causes to waste away or causes to diminish
scenarios.example_english: Disease causes his strength to waste away.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dīṅ kṣaye - divādiḥ ātmanepadī aniṭ. dīṅ-dhātuḥ apacayārthe kṣaye vartate. śyani kṛte dīyate iti rūpaṃ bhavati. lit-lakāre dide, dideṭe, didire ityādīni rūpāṇi.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dīṅ kṣaye - ātmanepadī divādiḥ. kṣayo nāma apacayaḥ. dīyate, dide. kṣīyate-tulya-artho bhavati.

meanings.English: to decay, to waste away, to diminish, to perish
meanings.Bengali: kṣaya haoyā, kṣīṇa haoyā, binaṣṭa haoyā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root gṛdh means to covet, lust after, or desire something greedily. In the basic Divadi active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject eagerly craves something. In the causative form (gardhayati), it means causing someone to desire or making an object covetable.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (Divadi shyan-vikarana)
scenarios.example_english: The greedy person covets another person's wealth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Gold tempts people (causes them to covet).

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'gṛdhu abhikāṅkṣāyām' under the Divadi class. Taking the shyan affix without guna of the vowel ri in Sarvadhatuka, it yields 'gṛdhyati'. It explains the optional nature of it-agama in certain Ardhadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'gṛdhu' conveys intense longing or covetous desire (abhikanksha). Forms like 'jagardha' in lit and 'gṛdhyati' in lat illustrate the regular application of Divadi morphophonemic rules.

meanings.English: to covet, to crave, to desire greedily

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rañj' primarily means to take color, redden, or become emotionally attached and delighted. In the Divadi group, it drops its internal nasal 'n' before the 'ya' vikaraṇa to form 'rajyati'. When used with a causative suffix (ṇic), it forms 'rañjayati', which means to color, dye, please, or entertain someone else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Divadi Parasmaipada kartari prayoga (drops internal nasal)
scenarios.meaning: becomes colored, becomes attached, takes delight in
scenarios.example_english: The sage takes delight in righteousness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic) Parasmaipada kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The king pleases his subjects with justice.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ranja rage' belongs to Divadigana. By Paninian rule 'rañjeśca' (6.4.27) or 'aniditām hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti' (6.4.24), the upadha nasal is elided before the sarvadhatuka 'syan' affix, yielding 'rajyati'. In non-kṅit or causative formations, the nasal is retained, producing 'ranjayati'. It denotes both physical coloring and emotional attachment.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'ranja rage' as taking the 'syan' vikarana with penile nasal elision (anidit-lopa), leading to forms like 'rajyati' in the 4th conjugation. The essential sense covers 'raga' (dyeing, affection, attraction, or redness).

meanings.English: to be colored, to redden, to be pleased, to be attached to
meanings.Telugu: rangu ponduta, anuragamu kaligi unduta, santoshapadata
meanings.Bengali: ronge roñjito howa, anurakto howa, anondito howa
meanings.German: sich farben, roten, Gefallen finden an, zuneigen
meanings.French: se teinter, rougir, s'attacher a, se plaire

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ādṛ' (ādṛṅ) belongs to the Divadi group (4th class) and takes the suffix 'syan' (-ya-) with Atmanepada endings due to its 'ṅ' marker. It primarily signifies respecting, revering, or paying earnest attention to someone. In the causative (nic), it means to cause someone to honor or receive respect.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Atmanepada with syan pratyaya and riṅ adesha)
scenarios.example_english: The student always respects the teacher.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic (Causative) in kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The king treats the scholar with utmost respect.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti confirms that ādṛṅ is always prefixed with an and has a svaret marker making it anit. By rule 'riṅ sye kiti' (P. 7.4.28), the root vowel undergoes 'riṅ' replacement before the 'syan' vikarana, deriving the base form 'ādriya-'. It is inherently Atmanepadi due to the ṅit anubandha.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that this root is strictly used with the upasarga 'an' in the sense of reverence and attentive care (adara). In active conjugation, it assumes Atmanepada suffixes (adriyate, adriyete, adriyante) and denotes focused mental regard or veneration.

meanings.English: To respect, to revere, to honor, to esteem, to pay regard to
meanings.Hindi: Aadar karna, samman dena, satkar karna
meanings.Bengali: Soddha kora, ador kora, samman janano

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kliś means to suffer, feel distress, or experience affliction. In its standard active form (Divadi gana with śyan suffix), the subject is experiencing distress or pain directly. When changed into the causative form (kleśayati), it means causing someone else to suffer or tormenting another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Divadi gana, śyan pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The person suffers due to misery.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya)
scenarios.meaning: Causes distress, torments, or troubles someone
scenarios.example_english: Diseases afflict and torment the body.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kliśū upatāpe divādau parasmaipadi. ūditvāt vā iṭ niṣṭhāyām. śyani rūpaṃ kliśyati iti bhavati. kleśaḥ santāpaḥ duḥkhānubhavaḥ vā upatāpaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kliśū upatāpe. upatāpaḥ duḥkhānubhavaḥ santāpaśca. kliśyati, kliṣṭaḥ, kleśitaḥ.

meanings.English: To suffer, to be distressed, to experience pain or affliction
meanings.Hindi: kaṣṭa pānā, duḥkha jhelnā, pīṛā sahanā
meanings.Bengali: kaṣṭa pāoyā, duḥkha bhog karā, kleśa pān
meanings.French: souffrir, être affligé, endurer la douleur

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'lus' belongs to the Divadi group (4th conjugation) and primarily conveys tearing, breaking, hurting, or damaging an object. It takes the conjugational marker '-ya-' (syan) and operates in the active voice (Parasmaipada) to denote inflicting injury or severance upon a direct object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present indicative, 3rd person singular, syan-vikarana)
scenarios.example_english: The hunter tears or injures the deer's body with an arrow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: karmani prayoga (passive present 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: is torn / is broken / is injured
scenarios.example_english: The fortress of the city is destroyed by the enemy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya commentary observes 'lusu bhedane' in the Divadi class. It conjugates with syan (ya-pratyaya) yielding lusyati. The semantic field implies splitting, cutting, or damaging parts of an entity. Forms such as lulosa, losita occur in respective non-conjugational tenses.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'lusu bhedane apakarane ca', highlighting the root's role in describing physical tearing, separation, or infliction of harm, conforming regularly to Divadi-gana inflectional rules.

meanings.English: to tear, injure, break, harm, or split

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhyai' means to meditate, contemplate, or think deeply about something. When conjugated in the active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes the subject actively engaging in deep mental focus or contemplation. When modified with the causative suffix, it describes making or inspiring someone else to meditate or reflect.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Lat Lakara (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sage meditates upon God in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to meditate / instructs in meditation
scenarios.example_english: The teacher guides the disciple to meditate on the truth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhyai cintāyām. divādiḥ parasmaipadī aniṭ. 'ādeca upadeśe'śiti' ityātve 'śyan'iti śyani dhyāyatīti rūpam. liṭi dadhyau. luṭi dhyātā. lṛṭi dhyāsyati. luṅi adhyāsīt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhyai cintāyām. cintanam dhyānam. dhyāyati, dadhyau, dhyātā, dhyāsyati. kṛdanteṣu dhyātaḥ, dhyānam iti prayogaḥ sādhyate.

meanings.English: To meditate, to contemplate, to reflect upon, to think deeply
